New Delhi: The rainy season in India technically ended on Wednesday, with the
summer (southwest) monsoon rainfall during June-Sept
period recording a deficit of
nearly 13% — a level of shortfall which is considered a drought. Significantly, this is the
fourth lowest seasonal rainfall since 2001 and the 13th lowest since 1901.

better during winter when
northeast monsoon hits south
Peninsular India between Oct
15 and Oct 21, with the IMD
predicting ‘normal’ rainfall
over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Karaikal, coastal Andhra
Pradesh and Rayalaseema region, Kerala and south interior Karnataka during OctDec period. However, the winter monsoon will bring cheer
to limited regions.

Though most other parts
of India are expected to receive ‘below-normal’ rainfall during the Oct-Dec period, some
areas of northwest India
(Punjab, parts of Haryana, Uttarakhand, Himachal and
J&K) and southern parts of

peninsular India are likely to
get “normal to above-normal”
rainfall. Incidentally, Punjab
and peninsular India had to
face huge rainfall deficit during the summer monsoon season, which led to drought in
many districts.

* THE TIMES OF INDIA, NEW DELHI
THURSDAY, OCTOBER 1, 2026
30
TIMES NATION

New Delhi: Upping the ante
against CEC Gyanesh Kumar
and PM Modi, the opposition
INDIA bloc Wednesday announced a month-long nationwide agitation starting Oct 2,
coinciding with the protest
call given by various student
bodies, including the Cockroach Janata Party, in Delhi and
states. Crucially, the opposition collectively demanded
that elections should revert to
ballot papers from EVMs, and
that pre-SIR electoral rolls be
restored for future elections.
It also sought an effective appeals mechanism for voters
excluded from the rolls. The
opposition has sought immediate resignation of the chief
election commissioner.

After deliberations, Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge announced that the six-day
agitation from Oct 2-8 would
start with district-level “save
democracy” protests. He said
opposition MPs will march to
the EC office in Delhi on Oct 6.

Moving forward, the alliance will hold five major rallies in cities during Oct-Nov, including a mega rally in Delhi
on Nov 1. The bloc appealed for
expediting SC cases pertaining to SIR and electoral malpractices. To mount pressure,
the opposition will seek to meet President Droupadi Murmu in Oct to brief her about
their concerns regarding SIR
and the Election Commission.

The meeting was attended
by Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi, Mamata Banerjee (TMC),
Dipankar Bhattacharya (CPIML), Omar Abdullah (NC),
Supriya Sule (NCP), Tejashwi
Yadav (RJD), M A Baby (CPIM), P Sandosh Kumar (CPI), K
C Venugopal (Congress), N K

Premachandran (RSP), Thol
Thirumavalavan (VCK), Uddhav Thackeray (Sena UBT)
and Hemant Soren (JMM).

The opposition has for
now paused the plan to submit
afresh removal notice against
CEC Gyanesh Kumar. Kharge
said the opposition agrees
that Kumar is working like a
puppet, with PM Modi and
Union home minister Amit
Shah pulling the strings.

Rahul Gandhi said he
told the leaders of the bloc
that they are the “collective
defenders” of the Indian
Constitution. “It is a personal commitment of all INDIA bloc leaders, we are going to ensure that people who
have destroyed Indian democracy are punished,” he said.

Trinamool Congress chief
Mamata Banerjee said, “We
demand that Gyanesh Kumar
must resign immediately. If
he is not removed, this movement can go very far..... We have to fight this battle together.” “Now it is clear, ‘Vanish
Kumar’ is ‘chor’ (thief), ‘daku’
(dacoit)... he has stolen votes,
burned, hijacked EVMs... rigged counting.... Gyanesh Kumar must resign immediately,” the former Bengal CM said, with Sonia sitting next to
her and lauding her remarks.

Rahul said there was a feeling in the room that the opposition had been successful
in convincing people that
elections are “stolen”. “There is a new sense of resistance, particularly among young
people, that what is going
on in India is wrong and needs to be stopped,” he added.

The 19 parties included
Samajwadi Party, CPI-ML,
JKNC, JKPDP, JMM, IUML,
KC(M), MDMK, VCK, KC(J)
and AIFB. RS MP Kapil Sibal
also joined Wednesday’s meet.

Announces ‘Save Democracy’ March From Oct 2 Seeking CEC Resignation

Amid SIR row, INDIA bloc puts up

united front, targets Modi, Shah

to ballot papers from EVMs, and that pre-SIR electoral
rolls be restored for future polls. It sought an effective
appeals mechanism for voters excluded from the rolls

New Delhi: Seeking to get
around the 2023 law shielding CEC Gyanesh Kumar
and two ECs, opposition may
seek FIRs against ECI functionaries not covered by immunity provisions, keeping
the watchdog in its sights for
allegedly “hijacking democracy”. The opposition has
decided to implead in the Supreme Court in the ongoing
challenge to the 2023
Act. The manoeuvre
will come even as the
India bloc will mount
pressure for repeal of
the immunity law.

Congress MP Rahul Gandhi
Wednesday
told INDIA bloc members
that the country will, 10-15
years later, remember them
as those who saved the
Constitution and democracy. He said BJP’s ruling system is falling apart and more govt “exposure” will happen in the next 6-8 months.
He said “collective resistance” is required to give one
more push to the system.

As the mood in the meeting was for agitation, suggestions were for marches and
dharnas, but CPI-ML’s Dipankar Bhattacharya stressed

the need to hit the iron hot.
He advocated a six-day action plan starting Oct 2, and
the proposal was adopted.

Crediting opposition unity in fighting “vote chori”,
Rahul said parties should
not lose sight of the national
perspective — like Congress
fighting the Left in Kerala
but being together in Delhi.

TMC chief Mamata Banerjee said Rahul Gandhi
can be “PM” and she has no
ego on this issue. Congress

chief
Mallikarjun
Kharge rebutted that
the fight is to save democracy, not for the
PM’s post. SP MP Harendra Malik urged
Congress, as “elder
brother”, to make sacrifices
over UP seat-sharing. He said regional parties can stall
BJP’s
march.
Uddhav
Thackeray urged Congress
to hold agitation with allies.

A few parties complained
of delay by Congress in convening the INDIA meeting after
the last one on June 8. Members stressed the need for a
“coordination committee”.

Tamil Nadu representatives pointed to the absence of
DMK, but Congress brass said it was in touch with the former ally. Sibal warned “delimitation” would be an issue.

without immunity

Ishita.Jairath@timesofindia.com

New Delhi: On Wednesday, TOI hopefully promised its readers that the travel
time from Mayur Vihar Phase-1 to AIIMS
will come down from 45 minutes to 15
minutes with the opening of BarapullahIII corridor. We hadn’t accounted for the
inability of officials to plan even for the
basics, it seems. On the first morning, as
hundreds headed towards the elevated
corridor, they found the much-touted
promise turn into a nightmare that
stretched to two hours, if not more.

Many commuters switched on Google Maps before starting their journey.
The app offered hope as it showed the
new route open. As many reached Mayur Vihar Phase-1, they found a small
hitch in the grand plan — the entry to
the corridor was still closed. Sanjay
Bhargava, a Mayur Vihar resident, said,
“Barricades were placed at the entry. So,
I took the conventional route. I did see
people coming in from the Noida Link
Road side, though,” he said.

The confusion soon shifted online.
“After 12 years, not even 12 hours and
it’s closed,” a commuter posted. Another
said that Google Maps was showing the
corridor as open even as 700 to 800 vehicles were stuck near its Mayur Vihar entry. Tagging PWD minister and CM, one
wrote, “What jokes are you playing with
the citizens of Delhi? The Barapullah
bridge inaugurated by the home minister
is closed for people on the very first day.”

Around 11am, the barricades were
removed. That was when the bigger headache began. Vehicles poured in and traffic quickly began piling up. The tailback
stretched towards Mayur Vihar, while the
exits towards DND and Ashram were also
choked. There was no breakdown holding
up traffic. There were simply too many
vehicles trying to use the same stretch
at once. Ishmeet started her journey at
1.30pm, expecting the non-peak hour to
work in her favour. It did not. “It took me
nearly 1.5 hours to cover 10km. I had to
take the DND exit and then return towards
ITO through the conventional Mayur Vihar flyover route. Ashram and Ring Road
were also clogged,” she said.

For many, it was just too much to handle as they started taking U-turns in the
middle of the flyover.

Kuldeep Singh Yadav, who was travelling on the stretch, said, “How can it get

choked on the first day? Earlier, I used to
take the Nizamuddin route, but Google
Maps showed this route today, so I decided
to try it. The problem does not seem to be
signage. It looks more like a road-design
issue, with traffic merging at certain
points. Like, the road narrows after crossing the river, while traffic also merges
from Ring Road and the Sarai Kale Khan
side. I feel this could become a daily
problem, with Barapullah-III ending up
like Pragati Maidan tunnel.”

Traffic police officers said no direction
had been issued to open the Mayur Vihar
entry in the morning. Traffic from NH-24
and DND also shifted to the new corridor,
with nearly 1 lakh vehicles entering the
stretch in a short span, they said. While
NH-24 and DND remained clear, Barapullah towards JLN Stadium choked as traffic
failed to disperse towards Ring Road. The
new corridor has three lanes against two
on the old carriageway, an officer said, but
balancing traffic will take time. The links
to DND and Ashram have added to the load.
Another said the project had been planned
12 years ago, based on traffic volumes at
the time. If the entire traffic of NH-24 and
DND shifts to the new corridor, congestion
could persist. Greater use of conventional
routes may eventually spread the load.

Meanwhile, PWD tents were seen occupying space on the other carriageway.
A road built to take traffic off Delhi’s congested routes had barely opened before
becoming a bottleneck itself.

The officers, however, said the carriageway from AIIMS towards Mayur Vihar
will be opened by Thursday afternoon.

On the initial barricading, they said,
“The confusion happened because the
person managing the tent was not cooperating. As soon as the issue came to our
notice, we immediately removed the barricades. Once traffic is opened on both sides,
the situation should ease as one set of
commuters will use the new route, while
others will continue using the DND-Ring
Road route towards east Delhi.”

PWD sources said completing the
decade-old project itself was a significant
step. “We can’t take responsibility for what
happened before we took charge. It is an
achievement that a stuck, dead project was
brought to life and finally opened. We can
answer for something we are starting from
scratch. If you ask us about the current
projects, we are planning for the next 30
years,” they said.

New Delhi: Paving the way
for Delhi to get a smart, technology-driven traffic management system over the next couple of years, the Union Cabinet Wednesday approved the
implementation of ITMS at an
estimated cost of Rs 1,789 crore. The project to be implemented by Delhi police will feature AI-enabled signals, realtime congestion detection, automated
enforcement
priority movement for ambulances across 42 key corridors.

The proposal for an Intelligent Traffic Management System (ITMS) was first initiated
ahead of the 2010 Commonwealth Games, though now the
scale has been expanded to use
the latest technology to detect
nearly 20 types of violations
and cover more stretches.

Announcing the decision,
Union I&Bminister Ashwini
Vaihnaw said the project will
add “brain” to Delhi’s traffic
management system as it will
make the city’s traffic management infrastructure “intelligent” by integrating existing
traffic signals, CCTVs, and AI
capabilities into a unified,
centralised control system.

PM Narendra Modi, in a
post on X, said the decision

will “ensure the usage of
technology to boost ‘Ease of

New Delhi: With an aim to draw up a long-term roadmap
for infrastructure creation and development in the capital, Union ministry of home affairs (MHA) has asked Delhi govt to prepare five-year capital investment plans.

The move seeks to shift the city’s development planning, which currently relies primarily on the annual
budget, to a long-term holistic plan.

According to MHA’s directions, reports have been sought from Public Works Department (PWD), urban development, transport, health and family welfare, education,
irrigation and flood control, environment and forest, power, industries, revenue, tourism, and training and technical education departments among others, an official said.

“The departments have been asked to look beyond
their immediate annual requirements and identify projects that could form part of Delhi’s infrastructure pipeline for the next five years. They will work on their respective plans by identifying areas where capital investment is needed the most and where such investments can
create long-term assets that will improve the experience
of people and improve their quality of life. The proposals
will then be submitted to MHA, which is expected to hold
a high-level meeting in the second week of Oct to review
them,” the official added.

Together, these departments are responsible for a large share of infrastructure creation undertaken directly
or through agencies of Delhi govt.

PWD is at the centre of Delhi’s public infrastructure
push. It undertakes construction, renovation and improvement of govt buildings and other public assets, including
roads and major structures under its mandate. The urban
development department deals with civic and urban infrastructure development and coordinates with multiple
agencies in case of projects that cut across departments.

While transport department is responsible for creating transport-related infrastructure, health and family
welfare department oversees govt’s public healthcare infrastructure like construction of hospitals and expansion and strengthening of existing healthcare facilities
that require substantial long-term investment. Education department carries out capital investment in construction and expansion of schools and educational infrastructure.

The irrigation and flood control department has a major role in flood protection and drainage infrastructure, which includes responsibilities like strengthening Yamuna embankments
and maintaining several major drains.

MHA’s involvement in Delhi’s long-term infrastructure roadmap is important because governance in the city is spread
across multiple authorities, and this multiplicity often creates
bottlenecks in carrying out development work.

“Since Delhi is a Union territory, MHA is the ultimate authority for all agencies here. That’s why its involvement is not
only likely to hasten the planning exercise but will also help in
timely execution of projects,” said the official.

Rekha Gupta flagged off 20 fire

Twenty specialised fire response motorcycles are for use in
narrow roads, crowded markets
and densely populated areas where large fire tenders may face difficulty reaching incident sites.

capacity of 100 litres of water
and 25 litres of foam. They have
a high-pressure pump capable
of generating at least 180 bar
pressure, a 60-metre high-pressure hose and a multi-system
nozzle with five modes.

“Delhi’s emergency services
are being continuously strengthened through better infrastructure, faster response capabilities, strategic deployment and
modern equipment. The capacity is being strengthened in phases,” said CM Gupta.

New Delhi: A shy boy from Jammu’s Kathua,
20-year-old Neeraj Bawa had come to Delhi a
year ago to fulfil his dream — a degree in economics from Delhi University. Today, he is fighting for his life in AIIMS Delhi, nearly a month
after the world came crashing down on him.

Neeraj was one of the three students
rescued after a PG collapsed in south Delhi’s
Satya Niketan on Sept 6. He is undergoing treatment after suffering lacerations on his stomach, back and near his groin, and a fractured
hip. After 26 days, six surgeries and multiple
skin grafts, Neeraj remains in Ward No. 9 of
the AIIMS ICU.

Five DU students — Arpit Jaj, Akshat Yadav, Pavan Yadav, Yuvraj Soni and Abhishek
Kumar — died in the building collapse.

Neeraj’s father, Darshan Dass (67), came to
know about his son’s injury from TV. “When I
turned on the news, a brief clip of a boy being
taken out from the rubble and placed on a
stretcher was playing. I thought the boy looked a lot like Neeraj,” he said. Neeraj’s sister
then identified the rakhi on his hand — she
had tied it on his hand just a week before.

The family was allowed to meet Neeraj a day
later, inside the ICU. “My boy immediately raised his hand to gesture that he was fine. He followed it with a raspy ‘main theek hoon papa’.”

Dass has remained outside Neeraj’s ward
since then. He feels his son will recover soon,
but “the doctors are uncertain. Till my boy is
in the ICU, no one can be sure.”

Many of Neeraj’s friends have tried, in vain,
to squeeze themselves during the one-hour visiting slot. “I didn’t know he made so many friends
in college,” said a pleasantly surprised Dass.

On Sept 6, Neeraj had just finished eating
lunch with his friend, Nitish Chib, when the
building collapsed. In despair, Neeraj called
his friends and sent them his live location, hoping they would pull him out soon.

Both were taken out hours later after a gruelling rescue operation and taken to hospital.
Nitish, who returned to his Jammu home after
being discharged, told TOI he could hear Neeraj pleading with his friends to save him while
they were trapped. The two had come to Delhi
together after securing a seat in Motilal Nehru College and decided to move into the PG.

“After getting into DU, I hoped to study
hard and do something worthwhile,” said
Nitish, “but I just don’t feel like coming back
to Delhi ever.”

Neeraj is worried he won’t be able to study
for a year because of his injuries. “Before he
left for Delhi, he told me he’d make me proud
one day,” said Dass. “I can wait for him to make
me proud, he just needs to recover and stand
up on his feet for now.”

Month On, A Father

Waits Outside ICU

IN HAPPIER TIMES: Neeraj Bawa (right) with his dad

GS.Dhanush@timesofindia.com

New Delhi: More than three
weeks after a five-storey PG
facility collapsed in Satya Niketan, killing five students
and two labourers, the neighbourhood is slowly slipping
back into its familiar rhythm.
Students can again be seen
sharing meals at fast-food
kiosks, sipping cold coffee or
gathering over tea and cigarettes. But the pile of rubble
where the building once stood remains a lingering sign
of the tragedy.

Residents claimed the student population is slowly
thinning out, with shopkeepers rueing their sales have
fallen by half. “The streets of
Satya Niketan used to feel
like a mela every day. It’s not
the same anymore,” said Pankaj, a cold-coffee kiosk owner.

According to a property
dealer, homeowners have also become wary of renting
out their properties after the
incident. “Given time, everything will go back to normal.
The students have no choice
but to come back here as, after
all, Delhi University does not
have enough hostels to accommodate them.”

For some students, proximity to colleges, 11-month
rent agreements and the
hassle of finding a decent flat
bind them to the area. In the
days after the collapse, while
many packed their bags and
left their PGs and flats, “some
of us cannot afford to leave
this place”, said Fiza Rizvi, a
student of Maitreyi College
who stays in a five-storey PG.

Following the tragedy, seven

people were arrested for failing
to take adequate safety measures during construction and repair work carried on and around the premises. According to
building regulations in Delhi,
no more than four storeys can
be constructed without stilt parking on the ground floor.

“I know the top floors have
been illegally built, but I can’t
just pack up and leave,” said Rizvi. If she chooses to leave before
her 11-month rent agreement
expires, she would have to forfeit the security deposit, which is
worth two months’ rent.

Sarthak Singwal, a sixth-semester student of Sri Venkateshwara, told TOI he has decided to stay in Satya Niketan as
he wants to focus on academics
rather than spending time hunting for a flat. “We came to Delhi
University with high hopes and
expectations. Future batches
will be apprehensive of choosing to study here,” he said.

Astudent of Jesus and Mary College, not wishing to be
named, said Satya Niketan
was the first location that popped up when she searched for
PGs online. “I cannot just shift
houses out of fear because something bad happened. A lot
of places in Delhi are unsafe,
so there is a lot to be considered before deciding anything.
But I will definitely find a place
somewhere else soon.”

New Delhi: For Darab Singh
(34), it was supposed to be another routine bike-taxi ride. On
Monday morning, he picked
up 22-year-old DU graduate
Hrishita Lahon from Sheikh
Sarai to take her to Noida. But
as they reached southeast Delhi’s Ashram flyover, the commute turned into a horrific tragedy that left Lahon dead and
Singh severely injured.

Singh remembers the bus
behind them, and then the impact. “A few minutes earlier, I
had left the bus behind. Then
the same bus hit us and dragged us along,” he said. According to Singh, he and Lahon
were dragged for 50-100 metres.

The only detail he clearly
remembers about the bus is
its colour — sky blue.

Singh said after the crash,
he could not see anything for
at least a minute. He could only hear voices around him.
When he regained consciousness, he saw Lahon lying near
the bike, bleeding.

“The bus was being driven
at high speed. I suffered injuries on my legs, knees and
hands. Both our helmets were
broken,” he said. “I was riding on the side, but the vehicle did not slow down.”

Singh said their phones
were thrown almost 10 metres
away due to the impact. Some
commuters picked them up
and kept them in their bags,
he recalled.

Then came a stranger
whom Singh remembers as one
of the first people to help them.

“A woman came… I remember her asking someone
to bring her car and taking us
to hospital. She kept speaking
to the injured woman in English,” he said.

Police learnt of the accident through a medico-legal
case (MLC) received from a
hospital around 12.58 pm. During the inquiry, they found
Lahon had been shifted to
another hospital in Sarita Vihar in view of her critical
condition. However, she succumbed during treatment
around 2.05pm. Her statement could not be recorded,

police officers said.

An officer said there was no
CCTV coverage on the stretch
of the flyover where the crash
occurred. A case was registered and police are still searching for the offending vehicle.

Singh, who has a daughter
studying in Class Vand a
son in kindergarten, had only
recently started working again. For nearly three years, he
had been unable to work because of worsening allergyrelated health problems and a
lung infection that had affected his ability to walk.

Wanting to support his family, he bought a motorcycle
on instalments in Jan and
started working as a bike-taxi
rider the following month. He
initially rode in Agra, his
native place, before starting
to work in Delhi in March.
Now unable to walk, he is staring at loss of income and an
uncertain future.

Singh survived Monday’s
crash, but Lahon did not. A
graduate of Maitreyi College,
Lahon had moved from Assam
to Delhi for higher studies. She
was pursuing a master’s degree in sociology from Ignou
and had joined an internship
programme just 20 days ago.

New Delhi: In an unusual limb-preservation procedure, doctors in Delhi
created a “green corridor” to transport a cancer-affected portion of the
thigh bone of an 11-year-old Uzbek girl
from one hospital to another for radiation treatment, before bringing it back
for reconstruction.

The girl, diagnosed with osteosarcoma of the left thigh, had already undergone eight cycles of chemotherapy
in Uzbekistan before arriving at Aakash Healthcare Super Speciality Hospital, Dwarka. Doctors removed the
affected portion of her femur as part
of a limb-preserving procedure.

Since radiation therapy was not available at Aakash, the excised bone was
transported by ambulance to Manipal
Hospital, around 3km away in Dwarka,
for radiation treatment. The bone’s dimensions had been shared in advance
so that an appropriate container could
be prepared for its transport.

The ambulance covered the distance in about seven minutes through the
green corridor. The radiation treatment took about 45 minutes, after
which the treated bone was transported back to Aakash in about nine minutes. The child remained in the operation theatre throughout the process.

The treatment strategy involved

removing the cancer-affected bone,
treating it with radiation to eliminate
residual cancer cells, and then reusing the child’s own bone for reconstruction. This allowed the doctors to
pursue limb preservation without exposing the child to the radiation required for treating the excised bone.

The transport was coordinated by
Puneet, the hospital’s security head, and
Ajit Pal from the medical administration
team, with the inter-hospital movement
planned to minimise the time taken for
the bone to reach the radiation facility
and return to the operating theatre.

Dr Aashish Chaudhry, managing director, Aakash Healthcare Super Speciality Hospital, said, “Complex cancer
care is not only about having every
specialised facility under one roof, it is
also about knowing how to bring the
right expertise together for the patient.
In this case, we created a green corridor
to take the affected bone to Manipal
Hospital for radiation therapy and
bring it back to Aakash for reconstruction. This required meticulous planning, coordination and surgical expertise, with every step designed around
preserving the child’s limb.”

The procedure was aimed at preserving the child’s own bone and the
function of her limb, rather than discarding the cancer-affected segment
after removal.

four-wheelers,

New Delhi: Monsoon rain may offer Delhi temporary relief from air
pollution, but it can’t stop emissions driving the city’s poor air quality, states a study by Centre for
Science and Environment (CSE).

Monsoon: Delhi’s baseline air
quality (2026), a study by CSE’s
Anumita Roychowdhury and Sharanjeet Kaur, examined air quality
during April-Aug 2026 to understand how much monsoon actually
improves Delhi’s pollution levels. It
argues that rainfall provides a natural “washout”, but pollution quickly returns once the rain stops.

Delhi’s average PM2.5 concentration fell from 60.2 micrograms per
cubic metre in April-May to 40.2ug/
m3 during the monsoon period in June-Aug, a decline of about 33%. But
the improvement did not translate
into consistently clean air. Of the 92
monsoon days, only one had good air
quality, while 53 days — 57.6% — were moderate and three poor.

The study analysed six separate rain events during the monsoon
to find that before rain, average
PM2.5 was 40.6ug/m3, which fell to

32.7 during rain, but rose to 36.2 within 24 hours and 45.1ug/m3 after 48
hours. The finding highlights a
central problem for Delhi: rain can
remove pollution from the air, but
it cannot prevent new pollution
from being emitted. As soon as the
rain stops, continuing emissions
from vehicles, industries, waste
burning and power generation can
rebuild pollution levels.

The problem also extends beyond particulate pollution. The
study found that when PM2.5 falls,
gaseous pollutants can become
prominent drivers of the daily air
quality index. Ground-level ozone
was prominent on 20% of the monsoon days, while nitrogen dioxide
was prominent on 10% and carbon
monoxide on 7% of these days. The
report links these pollutants to

emissions from vehicles, diesel generators and industries.

The authors warned that the
end of the monsoon removes this
natural cleaning mechanism just
as Delhi enters weather conditions that can trap pollution. Relying on seasonal rainfall or temporary winter restrictions is, therefore, inadequate, they said.

“While monsoon rains bring
temporary relief, they only mask
the underlying crisis. The fact that
even heavy rainfall failed to bring
consistent good air quality and
that pollution rebounded within 48
hours during dry spells shows that
our baseline emissions remain
dangerously high. As we enter winter, we are starting from a baseline
where continuous, elevated emissions will inevitably trigger severe
seasonal spikes,” said Roychowdhury, executive director of research and advocacy at CSE.

“Only sustained, year-round,
airshed-wide emission reductions
can secure cleaner air,” the report
states, calling for action across
transport, industry, waste management, electricity and other sectors across NCR.

New Delhi: A shy boy from Jammu’s Kathua,
20-year-old Neeraj Bawa had come to Delhi a
year ago to fulfil his dream — a degree in economics from Delhi University. Today, he is fighting for his life in AIIMS Delhi, nearly a month
after the world came crashing down on him.

Neeraj was one of the three students
rescued after a PG collapsed in south Delhi’s
Satya Niketan on Sept 6. He is undergoing treatment after suffering lacerations on his stomach, back and near his groin, and a fractured
hip. After 26 days, six surgeries and multiple
skin grafts, Neeraj remains in Ward No. 9 of

fallen by half. “The streets of

know about his son’s injury from TV. “When I
turned on the news, a brief clip of a boy being
taken out from the rubble and placed on a

On Sept 6, Neeraj had just finished eating
lunch with his friend, Nitish Chib, when the
building collapsed. In despair, Neeraj called
his friends and sent them his live location, hoping they would pull him out soon.

New Delhi: Chief minister Rekha Gupta Wednesday said ensuring women’s safety cannot be reduced
to imposing restrictions on girls and called for greater focus on the behaviour and upbringing of boys.
She also stressed the responsibility of police, civic
agencies and courts in making the capital safer.

Addressing the diamond jubilee celebrations of
Maitreyi College, Gupta said recent incidents of
sexual violence and harassment had once again raised concerns over women’s safety in the capital.

“In Delhi, we frequently hear of incidents that
cast doubt on the safety and security of girls. In such
situations, families often talk about imposing restrictions. But why only on girls?
What about the boys?” she said.

Referring to Prime Minister
Narendra Modi’s 2014 Independence Day address, Gupta said, “I
believe that our Prime Minister is
the only leader who, back in 2014,
spoke from the ramparts of the
Red Fort and asked: ‘You keep lecturing girls, but when will you talk
to the boys? When will you counsel the boys?’ It
shouldn’t even need to be said that no means no.”

The chief minister said responsibility for women’s safety extended beyond families and rested
equally with police, civic agencies, courts and society. She called for improved policing and better infrastructure, including adequate lighting, CCTV coverage and security personnel at vulnerable locations.

“The solution to women’s safety cannot simply
be to tell daughters what to wear, where to go or when
to return home. When daughters are given several
‘dos and don’ts’ in the name of safety, boys must also
be taught, with equal seriousness, about respect, responsibility, behaviour and consent,” she said.

“At times, girls hesitate to speak up because of
institutional or social pressure. Families, educational institutions, society, administration, police
and govt must work together to create an environment where daughters can speak fearlessly and
their complaints are taken seriously,” the chief
minister said.

Why only girls? Talk to
boys about responsibility,

respect and consent: CM

New Delhi: One-and-a-half
years after Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) built a
bamboo park on a five-acre reclaimed site at Bhalswa landfill and planted over 4,000 saplings, the park has disappeared, with the corporation
now using the site for dumping inert waste.

Multiple attempts to grow
bamboo at the site failed, following which a decision was taken to use the land for waste
processing and dumping, according to MCD officials.

“After a plantation drive
was completed in March last
year, the bamboo plants were
tended to for over a year. They
were regularly watered and
monitored. Despite these efforts, many of them could not
survive. A replantation exercise was carried out, but that
too failed as leachate (contaminated liquid) at the base of
the flattened landfill did not
allow the plants to grow,” one
of the officials said.

“After putting in a lot of effort to revive and maintain the
plantation, it was ultimately
decided, in view of operational
necessity for processing legacy
waste, to repurpose the site,”
the official said, adding, “We
have flattened a site close to the
entry of the site and will soon

use it for a fresh plantation.”

On Wednesday, TOI found
the land largely barren, with
wild bushes growing around
the park’s inauguration stone. The rest of the site was either vacant or covered with
heaps of inert waste.

The bamboo plantation
was launched in March 2025 in
the presence of chief minister
Rekha Gupta and then LG VK
Saxena. They described the
initiative as a significant step
towards creating a cleaner, greener and more liveable urban
environment in Delhi. The
plan then was to plant around
54,000 bamboo saplings in all.
However, a month later,
TOI reported that several saplings had started withering,

with officials citing soil conditions at the reclaimed landfill
site as unsuitable for their survival. A fresh plantation drive
was subsequently carried out,
and the Union minister for housing and urban affairs, who
adopted the site, visited it.

The issue was recently
highlighted by Praveen Kumar, former AAP MLA and
party co-in-charge in MCD.
“Officials at Bhalswa landfill
admitted that garbage was
again being dumped on 25
acres of land where a mountain of garbage had been removed during AAP’s tenure and
where bamboo saplings were
planted. On whose orders was
the plantation destroyed? Why
was garbage dumped again on
the cleared land? BJP should
stop misleading Delhi on the
issue of mountains of garbage,” AAP posted on X.

In June 2025, MCD planted
8,000 bamboo saplings on two
acres of reclaimed Okhla
landfill site, but that too
wasn’t a success. Grass was
subsequently planted there.

New Delhi: Stating that it wanted to make private taxi operators “accountable”, Delhi High Court Wednesday sought the stand of Centre, police,
Delhi govt and ride-hailing platforms Uber, Rapido and Ola Cabs on a plea seeking measures to
ensure the safety of women passengers using
app-based services.

“We want to make the private operators of the
taxi apps accountable. That is the reason we are issuing notices,” a bench of Chief Justice DK Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia said, while asking the
authorities and the companies to place their stand.
The matter has been listed for hearing in Dec.

Counsel for the petitioner contended that the
app-based operators were plying thousands of
cabs in the capital without adequate “checks” on
drivers, including whether they were under the
influence of alcohol during night hours.

In the plea, the petitioner raised several concerns regarding the operation of private cabs, including verification of drivers’ criminal antecedents, vehicle identification, route deviation,
emergency response, grievance redressal, preservation of electronic evidence and coordination between app-based transportation platforms
and law enforcement agencies.

The plea asserted that authorities should ensure surveillance and monitoring of public roads
and undertake a comprehensive review of the existing safety mechanisms and protocols for appbased transportation services. It also sought directions to mandate periodic and verifiable training of cab drivers on gender sensitisation, appropriate conduct towards women passengers,
prevention of sexual harassment and maintenance of personal boundaries.

The petitioner has also sought the establishment of 24x7 command-and-control centres to respond to SOS alerts.

Make taxi operators

accountable for
women safety: HC

New Delhi:A Delhi court has convicted a man for
insulting a woman’s modesty over the remark,
“Kaun se wale papa?”. The comment was made
when she told her three-year-old daughter that her
father had arrived to pick them up from school.
Though the two had no prior dispute, the court
held that the remark implied the woman had multiple partners and questioned the child’s paternity.

Judicial Magistrate First Class Moksha Bains,
in a Sept 24 judgment, said the remark was not an
innocuous inquiry about the child’s father but
carried an insinuation about the woman’s sexual
propriety and fidelity. “The expression, when addressed to a woman in the aforesaid setting, is not
an innocuous inquiry as to the identity of a person,” the judge said, adding that its “obvious insinuation” was that there could be more than one
man who could be described as the child’s father.

The case dates back to March 23, 2021, when
Priyanka Gupta was walking with her three-yearold daughter near RBI Enclave Gate in Paschim
Vihar. As the child cried, Gupta told her, “Dekho
papa aa gaye, don’t cry.” Girdhari Lal, who ran a
clothes ironing cart at a street corner, then allegedly interjected, “Kaun se wale papa aa gaye?”

Gupta initially ignored the remark and, about two minutes later, handed over the child to her
husband after he arrived in a car. She later informed her father-in-law, who called the police, following which an FIR was registered.

In his statement, Lal admitted making the remark but claimed it was not made with any “ill
intention”. Rejecting the defence, the court observed: “The explanation offered by the accused
that the words were spoken without ‘ill intention’ is a bare assertion. No surrounding circumstance has been brought on record from
which the remark could reasonably acquire an
innocent meaning.”

Why ‘kaun se wale
papa’ remark led to

man’s conviction

New Delhi: To improve security in its parks, MCD has directed senior officials of its horticulture department to conduct
safety checks at intervals of
one week to 15 days.

The corporation has also
initiated a comprehensive audit and provided its officials
with a field inspection proforma to be filled in within a week,
recording the latest condition
of the parks and covering 15 categories of safety parameters.

These steps are being taken
based on directions of LG T S
Sandhu. Work on some areas
has started, MCD officials said.

The measures to be taken
include checking illumination, obstruction of visibility
due to vegetation, presence of
abandoned or unused structures, condition of boundary
walls and entrances, uncontrolled entry points, lighting at
toilets and approaches, dark or
blind spots and thick bushes
that could conceal a person.

Ground staff and officials
have been asked to check safety
measures in children’s play areas and parking spaces, deployment of security personnel,
unauthorised gatherings or activities, whether a park is deserted, whether incidents of snatching, fight and harassment take place, and vulnerabilities arising from surrounding areas.

“We have found recurring issues plaguing the parks. Once

the survey is completed, preventive measures will be planned.
Meanwhile, directions have been given to officials for pruning
bushes and hedges, removing
green waste, repairing boundaries and entrance gates as a priority and coordinating with
other departments for proper
lighting,” said an official.

MCD has also readied a proposal for installing CCTV cameras at prominent points in 1,000
parks, deploying at least two security guards in each, putting
up boards displaying contact details of officials, and coordinating with Delhi Police for regular patrolling. The proposal will
be sent to Delhi govt, which will
examine its feasibility.

“Installing CCTV cameras is
not a challenge, but their operation and maintenance are. We
need proper logistics and a system for recording the feed. We
also need to determine the role
of RWAs; some may be interested in accessing the parks or taking responsibility for their maintenance,” the official said.

The project will require a
dedicated budget allocation.
The corporation has more
than 15,000 parks, of which around 15% to 20% are small. Security guards are currently deployed at only 43 parks spread
over two acres or more.

Shortage of horticulture
staff is another concern. There are around 4,100 staff, including about 3,000 contractual
multi-tasking staff, against
6,422 sanctioned posts.

MCD eyes safer parks
with CCTVs, patrolling

Vibha.Sharma
@timesofindia.com

New Delhi: Dark stretches around
women’s colleges, inadequate streetlighting and complaints of flashing
came under focus Wednesday as lieutenant governor TS Sandhu called for
plainclothes surveillance around
campuses and a real-time student safety app with emergency alerts and
GPS-based location sharing.

At a meeting with principals of
Delhi University’s 10 women’s colleges, LG directed Public Works Department (PWD) and Municipal Corporation of Delhi
(MCD) to repair streetlights
and install high-mast lights on
approach roads used by students, while ensuring adequate lighting and CCTV coverage
at bus stops and on public stretches. He also ordered the removal of objectionable graffiti
from college exterior walls and clearing of overgrown vegetation around
campuses to improve visibility.

On policing, Sandhu called for increased patrolling, PCR deployment
and picket-checking around colleges,
metro stations and isolated stretches,
particularly during morning and
evening hours. Additional personnel
and Pink booths were sought in areas
with high student footfall. Each college will have a nodal police officer to
coordinate on complaints involving
harassment, flashing and other safety concerns, backed by plainclothes
surveillance and an emergency response mechanism.

Safety audits around educational institutions were directed. Stationary buses parked near colleges,
which create obstructed and isolated stretches, are to be removed.

Principals and university officials
flagged several concerns, including erickshaws, autos and taxis soliciting
passengers and blocking college entrances, inadequate last-mile connectivity, encroached footpaths, unregulated vending, dark spots, unsafe parks
and public toilets near campuses.

LG directed MCD to remove
unauthorised encroachments and
vendors around colleges, men’s public washrooms and unauthorised
taxi stands adjoining boundary

walls, and relocate nearby
dhalaos. Parks near colleges
where drinking and substance abuse were reported were
to be secured.

On transport, Sandhu sought improved connectivity
between colleges and metro
stations
through
evening
shuttle services, U-Special
and metro feeder buses, besides dedicated pick-up and drop-off points for
e-rickshaws and autos. A mechanism
for reporting driver misconduct was
also sought. Police and the women
and child development department
were asked to jointly conduct regular
self-defence programmes, gendersensitisation workshops and awareness campaigns for students.

Sandhu directed DU and the higher education department to examine using govt accommodation as hostels and set up an inter-college women’s safety committee. He also sought uninterrupted mobile network
connectivity across college localities.

The meeting was also attended
by the DU vice-chancellor, senior police officers, transport, MCD and
PWD officials.

Cops in plainclothes,
safety app for students

LG Sandhu
CM Gupta

New Delhi: Delhi govt has approved a One Zone, One Operator
project worth Rs 17,969 crore, under which the city will be divided
into six zones and each will have
a single operator with end-to-end
oversight of sewer lines, manholes, pumping stations and complaints, water minister Parvesh
Verma said Wednesday.

In a DJB meeting, the Delhi
Water & Sewer (Tariff and Metering) Regulations, 2026, replacing
the 2012 rules, were approved.

The board also approved a Rs
6,044-crore project for transformation of south Delhi’s water
supply infrastructure, under
which smart meters with chlorine sensors will be installed.
“If there is a problem, the system should know about it, someone should be responsible for
fixing it, and the work should be
tracked till it is completed. That
is the change we want to bring,”
Verma said.

“The system will move from
reactive, complaint-based repairs to planned preventive maintenance, with geo-tagged inspections and real-time monitoring through a central command centre,” an official said.

DJB maintains 11,212 km of
sewer lines, 6.6 lakh manholes,
and 145 pumping stations. The south Delhi project will cover 247 sq
km and 2,44,381 domestic consumers. The One Zone, One Operator project is proposed to be financed by Centre (25%), Delhi
govt (25%) and a loan (50%).

Operator’ model
for sewage system

New Delhi: Stating that it wanted to make private taxi operators “accountable”, Delhi High Court Wednesday sought the stand of Centre, police,

ensure the safety of women passengers using
app-based services.

New Delhi:A Delhi court has convicted a man for
insulting a woman’s modesty over the remark,
“Kaun se wale papa?”. The comment was made
when she told her three-year-old daughter that her
father had arrived to pick them up from school.
Though the two had no prior dispute, the court
held that the remark implied the woman had multiple partners and questioned the child’s paternity.

“We want to make the private operators of the
taxi apps accountable. That is the reason we are issuing notices,” a bench of Chief Justice DK Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia said, while asking the
authorities and the companies to place their stand.
The matter has been listed for hearing in Dec.

Judicial Magistrate First Class Moksha Bains,
in a Sept 24 judgment, said the remark was not an
innocuous inquiry about the child’s father but
carried an insinuation about the woman’s sexual
propriety and fidelity. “The expression, when addressed to a woman in the aforesaid setting, is not
an innocuous inquiry as to the identity of a person,” the judge said, adding that its “obvious insinuation” was that there could be more than one
man who could be described as the child’s father.

Counsel for the petitioner contended that the
app-based operators were plying thousands of
cabs in the capital without adequate “checks” on
drivers, including whether they were under the
influence of alcohol during night hours.

In the plea, the petitioner raised several concerns regarding the operation of private cabs, including verification of drivers’ criminal antecedents, vehicle identification, route deviation,
emergency response, grievance redressal, preservation of electronic evidence and coordination between app-based transportation platforms
and law enforcement agencies.

The case dates back to March 23, 2021, when
Priyanka Gupta was walking with her three-yearold daughter near RBI Enclave Gate in Paschim
Vihar. As the child cried, Gupta told her, “Dekho
papa aa gaye, don’t cry.” Girdhari Lal, who ran a
clothes ironing cart at a street corner, then allegedly interjected, “Kaun se wale papa aa gaye?”

Gupta initially ignored the remark and, about two minutes later, handed over the child to her
husband after he arrived in a car. She later informed her father-in-law, who called the police, following which an FIR was registered.

The plea asserted that authorities should ensure surveillance and monitoring of public roads
and undertake a comprehensive review of the existing safety mechanisms and protocols for appbased transportation services. It also sought directions to mandate periodic and verifiable training of cab drivers on gender sensitisation, appropriate conduct towards women passengers,
prevention of sexual harassment and maintenance of personal boundaries.

In his statement, Lal admitted making the remark but claimed it was not made with any “ill
intention”. Rejecting the defence, the court observed: “The explanation offered by the accused
that the words were spoken without ‘ill intention’ is a bare assertion. No surrounding circumstance has been brought on record from
which the remark could reasonably acquire an
innocent meaning.”
The petitioner has also sought the establishment of 24x7 command-and-control centres to respond to SOS alerts.

New Delhi: Delhi High Court
Wednesday dismissed Umar
Khalid and Sharjeel Imam’s
third bail petition in the “larger conspiracy” case linked
to the 2020 Delhi riots, citing a
Supreme Court bar on relief
at this stage of trial.

The duo face anti-terror
charges under the Unlawful
Activities (Prevention) Act
(UAPA) in this case.

A bench of Justices Pratibha M Singh and Dinesh Bhatt
pointed out that the bench is
bound by “judicial discipline”
and can’t modify the Supreme
Court’s Jan 5 order asking the
two accused to seek bail either
on completion of examination
of the protected witnesses or
the expiry of one year, whichever is earlier.

“We would be modifying
this (Supreme Court) order if
we allow bail, which we cannot do,” the bench remarked.
The bench also said that the
duo can’t claim parity with
others in the riots case who
were granted bail since the
apex court had outlined a hierarchy of involvement.

The high court noted that
while denying bail to the two
accused in Jan, the apex court
had said that their roles were
distinct from the other co-accused and they were the “ideological drivers” of the alleged conspiracy.

“In view of the above discussion and the overall facts
of the case, specifically the
conditions imposed upon the

appellants, this court cannot
find fault with the decision of
the trial court. Accordingly,
the appeals are dismissed,”
the court concluded.

Khalid and Imam challenged the trial court’s July 4
decision rejecting their bail
pleas for the third time since
their arrest.

The trial court rejected
the bail applications, saying
it had “no option but to follow” the Supreme Court’s Jan
5 order and, therefore, could
neither entertain the plea nor
grant any relief.

The senior counsel appearing for Khalid argued that he
has spent six years in custody
and was entitled to be released on bail in view of a subsequent top court order giving
relief to other co-accused.

He added that around 10
months have passed since the
Jan 5 order and charges were yet
to be framed in the trial court.

Imam’s counsel also said
that he has been in custody for
six years and he was entitled
to bail considering the delay
in the conclusion of trial.

Additional solicitor-general SV Raju opposed the pleas
on behalf of Delhi Police and
asserted that the two are the
“masterminds” of the riots and
the Supreme Court has already
set a timeline for consideration
of any fresh bail pleas by them.

In Jan, the Supreme Court
granted relief to co-accused
Gulfisha Fatima, Meeran Haider, Shifa Ur Rehman, Mohammad Saleem Khan and
Shadab Ahmad.

New Delhi: For more than 20
years, Sadhana managed to
live away from prison where

said, 
she changed her name, moved cities and built a new life
as Pooja. Last week, Delhi Police’s crime branch arrested
her in Haridwar.

The case dates back to Jan
6, 1990, when the boy went
missing from Azadpur T-point. Police said witnesses Jagdish Chand and Vasdev had
seen Sadhana holding his
hand while crossing GT Road
around 5.30pm. Sadhana and
co-accused Raj Kumar were
arrested from Jahangirpuri.

The two were living together and the child’s father, Balwant Ram, and his family had
objected to it. A previous dispute led to resentment and a decision to take revenge, police said.

During the trial, Sadhana
was found to be the last person
seen with the child. Police said
she had also concealed Kumar’s presence at her house
and played an active role in the
conspiracy. She was convicted
under sections 302 (murder),
364 (kidnapping or abducting
in order to murder) and 120B
(criminal conspiracy) of IPC
and sentenced to life imprisonment. Sadhana was lodged
in Tihar Jail on Jan 9, 1990.

After spending years in jail,
Sadhana was released on parole on Dec 27, 2005, which was extended by three weeks on medical grounds. She, however, did
not surrender on Jan 18, 2006,
and began a second life.

She changed her name to
Pooja and moved through different places to avoid detection. Police said her final parole was arranged by another
Raj Kumar, a Tilak Nagar resident, on the reference of
Janki, a woman who was lodged with Sadhana in jail. Sadhana stayed with him before
taking up a job at a private
company in Noida.

There, she met Keshav, a
carpenter. They moved to Mukundpur, where they lived for
around five years before shifting to Haridwar. Police said
Sadhana married Keshav in a
temple and used his name as
her husband in documents,
helping conceal her identity.

Meanwhile, investigators
continued to pursue leads
through intelligence, old associates and family links. A recent lead about a woman living under an assumed identity took a team to Haridwar and
Sadhana was arrested on Sept
27. Her years of borrowed independence came to an end as
she was sent back to jail.

New Delhi: Applying its recently
framed policy of rejecting challenges to bails granted by high courts,
Supreme Court Wednesday told
West Bengal govt it would dismiss
the state’s appeal against grant of
interim bail to Milan Pradhan,
Congress candidate for the Nandigram assembly bypoll, who is an accused in a 2007 murder case.

The CJI Surya Kent-led
bench expressed difficulty
in listing the matter for
Thursday and said, “Instead of Thursday, we will dismiss the appeal Monday.”
By Monday, electioneering for the
bypoll would be over and the state’s appeal would be infructuous.

Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the state, requested the apex court for a hearing on
Thursday of the appeal challenging grant of interim bail to Pradhan for canvassing for the election scheduled for Oct 6, campaigning for which will end on Oct 4.

When the bench said since the
high court had granted only interim bail, it would not entertain
such an appeal, solicitor general
Mehta brought up Pradhan’s history sheet — accused in a murder
case and featuring in six other
FIRs on serious crimes — to request a hearing on Thursday.

The HC had, citing the relief SC
gave to AAP functionary Arvind
Kejriwal, granted bail to Pradhan
Tuesday and asked him to surrender before the additional chief judicial magistrate, Haldia, on Oct 21.

Counting of votes in Nandigram constituency, which was

vacated by chief minister
Suvendu Adhikari who also won from Bhabanipur,
will happen on Oct 9.

The state said in its appeal, “The HC granted interim bail to Pradhan, an
accused charged with multiple
counts of heinous offences including murder, arson, bomb
blasts and rioting with deadly
weapons, solely on the untenable pretext of permitting him to
participate in an election.”

It added, “The HC completely
disregarded settled principles governing grant of bail, overlooked
the respondent’s continuous evasion of judicial process for nearly
two decades, ignored his active
subversion of the criminal justice
system, and exposed prosecution
witnesses to imminent danger.”

nothing less than capital punishment for both the accused.”

proceedings,

A thought for today


o you feel you would have lived
life better if you had known
so many things you did not
know then? How many more painful
lessons would you have to learn to live
a fulfilled life? What if you could learn
to live wisely, without having to go
through suffering?

You get weighed down with worry,
anxiety, and grief. Is the world giving
you sorrow? Or could it be that you
have not learnt the technique of
dealing with the world?

Gita gives knowledge of the world,
yourself, and art of right contact with
the world. It begins with Arjun’s grief.
Arjun, mighty warrior, accomplished
archer, and commander of Pandav
forces is overwhelmed and unable to
act. Krishn does not console Arjun.
He gives him knowledge. As Arjun’s

understanding deepens, his confusion
disappears. At the end of Gita,
he rises, fights the battle, and
wins. The battlefield has not
changed. Arjun has.

Life is misleading. The
road to heaven feels like
hell. And the road to hell
is heavenly. One demands
discipline. The other rewards
temptation. One asks you to
be patient. The other whispers
–take the easy way.

Sense enjoyment gives
pleasure. So, you indulge in
it indiscriminately. But the
law of diminishing returns
functions. The more you
indulge the less you enjoy.
The answer is not rejection,
but regulation.

We believe selfishness is the way to
go. Yet thought of self is the greatest

learn the rules of the game. However
talented you may be, if you don’t know
the rules you lose. You have entered
the arena of life. Do you know the
rules of the game of life?

The world is a mix of pairs of opposites.
It is in a constant flux of change. And
the change is unpredictable. In short,
the world is undependable. Everything
in the world is passing, ephemeral,
finite. Yet you project a false sense of
permanence on the world. And are
heartbroken when it goes.

Possess the world, enjoy it fully.
But never depend on it. Amid this
kaleidoscope of change, do what you
have to do. Play your part to the best
of your ability. With sincerity and
dedication. And you will grow to the
state of spiritual awakening.

It’s been over 17 months since Pakistan closed its airspace to

Indian airlines, and costs have piled up. The first 12 months cost
Air India alone some `4,000cr. While longer flight durations,
extra fuel burn, and staff expenses are a headache, loss of market
share to foreign airlines – who aren’t banned over Pakistan – is also
a concern now. DGCA’s data for April-June this year shows total
passenger volumes to and from India are down 9.1% y-o-y, but
foreign airlines’ market share has risen from 53.8% to 62.7%. This
can’t go on, and considering how Pakistan has repeatedly shut its
airspace to India’s carriers over the years, waiting for it to back off
isn’t an option. Instead, viable alternative routes must be found,
and Air India, IndiGo, and GOI are already working on it.

As TOIreported Wednesday, India is trying to work out a Pakistan
bypass via China for its airlines. The proposed route lies over Hotan

in northwestern China’s Xinjiang region. While
this still involves a detour, it’s not as long as
circling Pakistan to get to Europe or North
America from airports in Delhi, Amritsar, and
Lucknow. And for Central Asian destinations
like Tashkent and Almaty, the Hotan route could
be as good as flying over Pakistan. Last year, an
Indian carrier had suspended flights to these
two cities briefly because flight durations had doubled.

The other option, as the aviation minister has suggested, is to fly
more westward routes out of southern airports that are not affected
by the Pakistani airspace closure. With recent improvements in
India-China ties – EAM Jaishankar spoke about it in New York on
Monday – the Hotan route is possible, and as the aviation minister
has said, “Diplomatic level talks are underway.”

At a time international air travel growth is averaging 5% annually,
Indian carriers can’t be losing market share. But the circumstances
are beyond their control. Before the airspace closure, about 20%
of their international flights crossed Pakistan. Overnight, flights
to the same destinations became 47 minutes longer, on average. And
those to San Francisco and Vancouver, for example, became up to
four hours longer. This year, Iran war has pushed up jet fuel costs,
so Indian carriers are not only flying longer routes, but also paying
more per mile. So, foreign airlines – overflying Pakistan as usual –
have a huge cost advantage. An alternative route would be a win
for Indian business and diplomacy.

On Sept 18, Warren Buffett
stepped down as chairman
of Berkshire Hathaway
at 96, ending a run that
began in 1970. While
tributes have dwelt on
his returns, they should focus on the
man, because his habits have outlasted
holdings – and matter more now in an
age of apps, algorithms, and influencers.
Six lessons stand out.

Rejection is not a verdict | Buffett was so
certain of a seat at Harvard Business
School that he urged a friend to join him
there before he’d even been accepted. A
10-minute interview ended that. He later
called Harvard’s rejection the pivotal
episode of his life, because it redirected
him to Columbia, and into his hero
Benjamin Graham’s classroom.

Rejection today arrives faster and
more publicly: an algorithm screens
out a CV, a layoff lands by email, a feed
shows peers announcing promotions
you didn’t get. Buffett’s example isn’t
“never give up” – that’s a platitude. It’s
narrower: a closed door is a measure of
the target, not the archer, so re-aim.

Audit your mistakes |At 11, Buffett bought
three shares of Cities Service Preferred,
plus three more for his sister Doris, with
money he’d saved since age six. The
stock fell from $38 to $27, and Doris
reminded him of it every day on the
walk to school. He sold at $40 for a small
profit, then watched it run to $202. He
called it one of his life’s most important
episodes, and extracted three rules that
shaped six decades: don’t anchor on
your purchase price, don’t grab a small
profit to quiet your nerves, and don’t
manage other people’s money unless
you are certain.

Modern trading apps are engineered
to prevent exactly this reflection – every
tap delivers instant feedback, and the

next trade is one swipe away. Results are
measurable. SEBI found 91% of individual
F&Otraders in India lost money in FY25,
with net losses near `1.06L cr. Most treat a
loss as bad luck and move on. Buffett treated
it as tuition, and kept the notes.

Keep an inner scorecard | His father,
Howard, judged himself only against
his own standards. Buffett called him
“a 100% Inner Scorecard guy,” warning
that anyone who lives for the world’s

opinion “will wind up with an Outer
Scorecard”.

The outer scorecard now comes
with a live dashboard: likes, followers,
a friend’s screenshot of gains on the
stock you skipped. In 1999, Buffett
was mocked as a relic for missing the
dotcom boom. He didn’t flinch; within
two years the mockery reversed. The
same discipline let him run a “Mistake
Du Jour” section in his annual letters –
confessions most executives bury. In
an era that rewards looking right, he
optimised for being right.

Want less, be patient | The Buffett family
motto might have been “spend less than
you make,” with the corollary “don’t go
into debt”. Buffett lived for decades in
the house he bought in 1958, and took a
hamburger over anything fancier.

This isn’t a sermon on thrift; it’s a
point about power. Lifestyle creep, easy
EMIs and buy-now-pay-later schemes
convert future income into present
obligations. Someone carrying heavy
fixed costs cannot afford to wait – and

waiting was Buffett’s entire edge. A man
who needs little money is never forced
into a bad decision to get more of it.
Desperation is expensive.

Be sceptical of incentives | At 10, on a
visit to Wall Street, Buffett met Sidney
Weinberg of Goldman Sachs, who asked
him, “What stock do you like, Warren?”
Weinberg forgot the exchange by the
next day. Buffett remembered it forever,
and spent his life paying the courtesy
forward under his own rule: “praise
by name, criticise by category”.

Yet, warmth never dulled his scepticism
of incentives: “Don’t ask the barber
whether you need a haircut,” he liked to
say, a line that has never been more useful.
The finfluencer with an undisclosed
tie-up, the app that profits from your
trading volume, the adviser on commission:
all barbers. Listen politely, then ask
who gets paid if you say yes.

Find your Charlie Munger | Buffett’s most
valuable partnership began with long
phone calls to a Los Angeles lawyer.
When Munger’s wife asked why he paid
such attention to this Omaha fellow, he
said simply: “That is no ordinary human
being.” For six decades, Munger’s real job
wasn’t to agree with Buffett, it was to tell
him when he was wrong. Buffett credited
him with the habit of studying failures,
instead of admiring successes.

The modern world makes this harder
by design. Algorithms serve up people
who already agree with you; group
chats reward consensus over correction.
Even AI assistants, left unchecked, can
drift towards telling users what they
want to hear. Everyone needs at least
one sparring partner sharp enough to
say “that’s a dumb idea”, and trusted
enough to be heard.

Early in Buffett’s career, a member of
a prominent Omaha family predicted
over lunch that the young upstart would
be broke within a year. Seventy years on,
Berkshire is up 6,099,294%. The returns
were the by-product. The character
was always the point.

For the nth time, Supreme Court has held a case of preventive

detention illegal, and fined, this time, UP govt Rs 10L. SC imposed
the fine for “blurring…the distinction between punitive and
preventive jurisdictions, in substance.” The unfortunate reality is,
authorities blur this distinction in a case too many. Special laws such

allows bail. Courts have repeatedly held that authorities/ govts can’t
keep individuals in lockup/ jail under these laws, where the apparent
objective is to ensure undertrials don’t stand a chance at bail. Routine
criminal law, allowing bail, would suffice in many of these cases.

Courts have held special laws give the executive
extraordinary power in stringent provisions, but
only within tightly defined boundaries.

Allahabad HC had also held govt failed to
distinguish between areas of law & order, and
public order. If the petitioner was likely to harm
law & order only, and not impact public order, then
detention under NSA wasn’t legally sustainable.
Similarly, J&Kquashed a PSA detention last year,
because authorities combined two grounds, when the law separates
them – acting against security of state, and acting against public order.
The difference between law & order, and public order, is not rocket
science. What Justice Hidayatullah (Lohia v Bihar 1966) held decades
ago bears repeating: “Imagine three concentric circles… ‘Law and
order’ represent the largest circle within which is the next circle
representing ‘public order’ and the smallest circle represents ‘security
of state’… An act may affect law & order, but not public order, just
as an act may affect public order, but not security of state.”

In case after case, courts have found legal error with preventive
detention under special laws. They’ve held that govts stretched
their exceptional powers beyond the statute, that requirements
for preventive detention weren’t met. That authorities have been
fined in such a case is a timely wake-up call.

Earning appreciation and awards at the
world’s most respected film festivals,
then struggling for a domestic release
–this has been the story of independent
cinema in India for years.

The past fortnight alone perfectly
illustrates this truth. Angh, a Konyak-language feature
from Nagaland by debutant director Theja Rio, won
the Platform Prize at the recently concluded Toronto
International Film Festival (TIFF) 2026.

According to new rules announced this year by
US’s Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences,
a non-English language Platform Prize winner at
TIFF gains automatic entry into the race for the
Best International Feature Oscar. TIFF is one of just
a handful of global festivals from where a winner
of a prize identified for the purpose gets this added
benefit – earlier, the only route to this particular
Oscar category was for a film to be selected as its
country’s official entry.

Even as India celebrated Angh’s triumph, director
Rima Das’s Village Rockstars 2 arrived in theatres
across the country. These simultaneous developments
do not in any way indicate that the hurdles formerly
faced by Indian indies have been cleared from their
paths. On the contrary, Das has had an arduous
journey with this Assamese film.

Her experience is a sobering reminder that
those who prioritise their artistic commitment and
independent spirit over commercial considerations,
and have consequently drawn the international
spotlight to India repeatedly over time, are forced to
fight numerous battles to reach a domestic audience
beyond festivals.

Their story after the glory | Village Rockstars 2 is
the sequel to Das’s acclaimed breakout film, Village
Rockstars, which premiered at TIFF in 2017, won the
National Award for Best Feature Film, and was India’s
Oscar entry the following year. It was a charming
saga of a girl growing up in rural Assam. In 2024, Das
premiered Part 2 at Busan International Film Festival,

where she bagged the coveted Kim Jiseok Award. It
has taken two years for Village Rockstars 2 to reach
Indian theatres, that too in a staggered fashion – it
was released in Assam this March, and is only now
running outside Das’ home state.

In a year filled with accolades for Indian indies, it is
tempting to look away from the difficult conversation
about what happens after a victory on a prestigious
world platform. The crop of honours reaped by India’s
independent filmmakers in the first half of 2026 alone
include the Best Film Award at Moscow International

Film Festival for Fazil Razak’s Malayalam venture
Moham (Desire), along with the Best Actress trophy
for its lead, Amrutha Krishnakumar, and a Crystal
Bear Special Mention for Das’s Not A Hero at Berlin
International Film Festival. Yet the truth is that both
Moham, which premiered at the International Film
Festival of Kerala 2025 where it won an award, and
Not A Heroare yet to be released in India.

Short sight, short shrift |Those who argue that market
forces should be left to determine which films get space

in theatres must be reminded that India’s big-banner
productions have been flopping in large numbers in
recent years, yet distributors and exhibitors still avoid
betting on indies. The few indies that are released
are set up for commercial failure by the system. They
are relegated to suburban theatres and odd show
timings. Even when a film has been subtitled by its
producer, theatres routinely skip playing subs. They
also do not promote indies.

Such films usually have sparse marketing budgets,
which makes it near-impossible for them to combat

these unfavourable circumstances, but if they don’t
fill halls from Day 1, they are removed before word of
mouth from early viewers can spread. It’s a Catch-22
bind, since streaming platforms have begun acquiring
films based on theatrical performance.

Second guessing the public | All-round myopia
on the business side is more exasperating now than
ever before, because a significant number of viewers
have become increasingly adventurous in their film
choices, due to exposure to an unprecedented variety
of cinema in the streaming era.

An Independent Filmmakers Association of
India (IFAI), formed earlier this year, aims to
correct this situation. As it gets off the starting
block, IFAI must ensure that it does not mirror the
inequities filmmakers already deal with outside
the organisation.

If it is to genuinely represent India’sindie cinema,
it must rope in and equally back those working in
all languages and states, in addition to filmmakers
from marginalised and minority communities.
This would enable a greater understanding of unique
problems, including social prejudice and distinct
economic
obstacles
faced
individuals,
challenges before filmmakers in conflict zones, or in
states with limited to nil infrastructure for filmmaking
and screenings.

Independent cinema has brought glory to India for
years. It is inexplicable and inexcusable that Indian
audiences are largely denied access to these films
beyond the festival circuit. Any move to improve this
scenario merits attention.
