TIMES Special

Amarjeet.Singh@timesofindia.com
Is the north India problem
moving to central India?
And, consequently, could
farm fire haze become an
autumnal headache for cities in the west and east too?

Madhya Pradesh has emerged
as a third node in a stubble-burning
triad, recording more fires than
Punjab and Haryana in 2024 and
2025. It’s not that farmers in the central Indian state have suddenly

started burning more stubble.

MP’s farm fire numbers
have largely held steady over
the years but have become
conspicuous now because of the
steep fall in fire counts in Punjab
and Haryana. In 2025, MP recorded 17,067 paddy-residue burning
events, more than three times
Punjab’s 5,114.

Punjab and Haryana fires,
however, have a direct bearing on
Delhi’s pollution load because of
wind direction and meteorological factors. MP’s are less so for
Delhi, but a bigger concern for
downwind cities.

Data compiled by Consortium for Research
Agroecosystem
Monitoring
Modeling from Space
(CREAMS), which is
part of ICAR-IARI
that records the official farm fire count
through satellite imaging, shows MP’s
wheat-residue burning has become a
major concern, too.
After declining from
27,759 incidents in
2022 to 13,665 in 2024,
the number jumped
to 34,429 in 2025 and
39,165 in 2026. The
2026
number
more than 50% of
the 68,259 incidents
detected in Punjab, Haryana, UP,
Delhi and MP between April 1 and
May 31. Vidisha, Siddharthnagar,
Hoshangabad, Raisen and Ujjain
were the hotspots.

A large agrarian state, MP’s paddy acreage area is more than double that of Punjab. And it’s increasing because of climatic factors like
more erratic rainfall events and
flooding of farms that have left the
state’s other major crops like urad
and soybean vulnerable. Farmers,
therefore, are switching to waterintensive paddy, which gives more
yield. The crop residue problem, as
a result, is also growing.

To tackle this, MP needs the
same interventions as Punjab and
Haryana, but on a much wider
scale, making this a serious administrative challenge. Farmers said
— citing labour shortages, rising
input costs, unsuitable machinery
and the absence of a viable market
for residue — that burning cannot

be tackled simply through penalties
or awareness, .

“In the entire Vidisha district,
we mainly cultivate Sharbati variety of wheat. We do not have good
irrigation. Only one portion of the
district is connected with canal irrigation. Thus, if the residue is not
burnt and left in the farm, the soil
becomes hard. Labour shortage is
also there,” said Vidisha farmer
and Kisan Congress district president Vineet Dangi.

Many farmers cannot access
subsidised machinery like harvesters and happy seeders. “The
schemes are there, subsidies for
buying required equipment are
there, but they are mostly absent
on the ground and have not been
popularised. If each panchayat is
provided with two or three seeder
machines that are available for
rent, farmers will not go for burning,” Dangi added.

“Stubble
removal
increases
costs for us,” said Vishnu Pratap
Dangi, a Vidisha farmer. “The most
practical solution is to create value
for the product. If stubble becomes
valuable, farmers will do everything possible and will not burn it.”

In
Vidisha,
district
administration has proposed an
industrial
route
turn crop residue into
a resource. Indian Oil
Corporation has begun setting up compressed biogas (CBG)
plants in the district.
Govt land is being

identified for the proposed plants.

MP’s deputy director for agriculture, R K
Singh, said equipment
availability is govt’s
main focus this year.
“We have made available equipment to farmers at a large scale.
We will also register
all big harvester machines coming
to the district during the season,
and only those having the required
equipment to ensure that stubble
is not left behind will be allowed to
work,” he said.

State president of Bharatiya
Kisan Union (Tikait) Anil Yadav
said enforcement alone would not
work. “No farmer wants to create
pollution or adversely affect nature.
Farmers are the ones who are closest to nature. Govt should make arrangements for procuring stubble
from the farm itself,” he said.

In Sheopur, farmer Anil Singh
Jaat of Talawada said solutions
also need to be tailored to local
conditions. He cited subsidised
super seeders that farmers purchased but which, he said, were
unsuitable for the area’s hard
soil.
“Technical
interventions
and solutions should be localised.
One solution for everywhere is
not possible,” Jaat said.

Neel Kamal | TNN
It’s early days in the stubble-burning
season – which autumn has come to be
called in Delhi-NCR because farm fires
have for years turned its pre-winter airshed into a choking haze – but the signs
from Punjab are encouraging.

Come Sept, swirls of smoke rise from its
vast expanse of paddy fields. But the state,
which along with Haryana has been blamed
for Delhi’s winter smog, has turned a corner
over the last few seasons. Farm fires have
dropped sharply in Punjab, from more than
83,000 recorded in 2020 to around 5,100 in 2025.
Early signs are that the trend will continue
this year, with just about two dozen stubbleburning cases recorded so far this season compared to 80-odd in the same period last year.

While govt has helped procure the machinery needed for stubble management, farmers
determined not to burn stubble represent the
state’s real change, says Preetinder Pal Singh,
sarpanch of Ransih Kalan village, 35km from
Moga.“Farmers of our village took a pledge
not to burn stubble. We are not only keeping
our word but also persuading nearby villages
to follow suit,” said Singh.

A part of the fall in Punjab’s farm fire numbers has been attributed to farmers burning
stubble at night to circumvent satellites that
record data. Ground realities, however, don’t
back this. This correspondent has been reporting from Punjab for four decades and would
find it hard to travel through Sept and Oct because of smoke from the fields. Over the last
couple of years, smoke from fields that would
hang over roads, highways and villages has reduced significantly.

Agriculture department director Gurjit
Singh Brar said, “In an era when everything
is tracked, is that (concealing stubble-burning)
even possible to do? That too across the whole
state? There are several reasons for lower stubble-burning. The main reason is farmers can
make money from selling the residue to pellets
and briquette units (which convert it into biomass for use as industrial fuel)”.

Punjab agriculture minister Gurmeet
Singh Khudian said farmers have already procured 16,227 crop residue management (CRM)
machines for this season, and the state has released a subsidy of Rs 183 crore to buy 10,000

CRM machines. But success isn’t guaranteed.
Farmers need resources to procure the CRM
machines and burning paddy straw remains
the quickest way to clear a field for the rabi
crop. Only 1% of Punjab farmers has the
means to access equipment by renting from
custom hiring centres. This leads to a dependence on informal borrowing but less than 20%
farmers have access to cooperatives.

That’s why farm organisations have been
demanding cash incentives to manage crop
residue. “Many farmers have no option but
to burn stubble as they have no resources to
manage it. Even if machinery is provided,
they have to arrange for tractors and shell
out money on diesel to run tractors. Supreme
Court has asked govts to provide compensation to farmers so they may desist from

stubble-burning, but govt is yet to do so. We
reiterate our demand,” said Hajinder Singh, a
farmer from Baggi village in Bathinda. Gora
Singh from Bhainibagha in Mansa said farmers have started adopting modern methods to
manage stubble in the fields but want compensation to sustain it.

Farmers in Punjab grow three crops a
year. After harvesting wheat in winter, they
grow maize, which matures in 70 days and
is mainly used as ‘bio achar’ (alternative to
green fodder) The paddy crop that follows is
transplanted mid-July and matures late Oct,
leaving little time for sowing of wheat.

This cycle continues.
A section of farmers did shift to shorter varieties of paddy after govt mandated that paddy
transplantation would have to begin from June
15, but many farmers still grow the longer varieties — primarily Pusa 44 — because of higher
yields. These also generate more stubble
residue. Crop diversification to break the
wheat-paddy cycle, and consequently
reduce paddy stubble, has not taken
off. Cotton was Punjab’s third major crop but its acreage has been
declining because of pest attacks
like white fly and pink bollworm.
From over 3 lakh hectares a
decade ago, cotton has shrunk
to under 1 lakh ha. This year,
paddy area is around 32 lakh
hectares, 80% of the total cultivable area of the state. The total
straw generated is estimated at
19 million tonnes.
As long as this continues,
there will be stubble. And stubble
will need exhaustive management
each year to prevent farm fires. CM
Bhagwant Mann has called for collaboration with Confederation of Indian
Industry to accelerate sustainable crop
residue management. During a recent meeting with a CII delegation, Mann said, “There
is a need for govt, industry and other stakeholders to work together to ensure that farmers get practical, affordable and effective solutions,” he said.

The state govt has prepared an action plan
to spread awareness among the farming community against stubble-burning. Around 151
blocks have been identified in its 23 districts.

Ipsita.Pati@timesofindia.com
At Bhuthan Kalan in
Fatehabad, the district that saw most
crop stubble fires in
Haryana
last
year,
balers (machines that compress
loose, bulk residue into dense,
bound blocks) have reached a section of small farmers this year.
At Mohammadpur Rohi, another
village in the district, Mahinder
Singh has started a straw pickup
business this year. He has 13 tractors, which cover around 30 acres a
day, and deliver the cargo to factories — bottlers, cardboard makers,
dyeing units and others who use
it for different purposes like biomass fuel and cushioning. “There
are more than 30 factories in this
area that are buying straw bales. I
am charging Rs 200 per quintal for
paddy straw,” says Singh.

In Suniyana, at the farms of
Gureninder and Bajinder Singh,
who own 90 acres between them
in Fatehabad, combine harvesters
have already cleared the first batch
of paddy and multiple balers have
been deployed to clean up. The
stacks wait for pickup tractors like
Mahinder Singh’s to arrive.

Govt data says there are 9,000
more machines that are ready for
deployment this year — among
them happy seeders, balers, hay
rakes, crop reapers and rotary
slashers — for harvesting, sowing

and in-situ paddy management.
In a state that brought down farm
fires last year to around 600, there
is hope that the last-mile gap in
stubble management can be overcome in the next couple of seasons.

The optimist view is that the
state can become farm fire-free in
the near future. The cautious
view is that stubble will continue to be a challenge year
after year till farmers can
be convinced to move away
from wheat and paddy. Total
paddy acreage in Haryana is
around 16 lakh hectares this
year and the estimated crop
residue is 80 million tonnes.

Mahinder Singh said he
does not charge farmers to
remove their straw because
he earns from selling it. “I am
doing this work for the first
time. I am not charging farmers as I am earning from the
stubble. I make bales and sell
them to companies,” he said.

He expects the arrangement to reduce burning in
the villages. “There will be
no stubble-burning this year
in at least 10 villages that I am providing service in,” he said, adding
that others had also started similar businesses.

Agriculture
official
Girish
Nagpal said the market was developing through different arrangements between farmers, aggregators and industrial buyers, though

it remained informal. “This is an
unorganised field so far,” he said.
Some companies, he explained,
place orders with aggregators,
who collect the required quantity
from farmers. “They come and
tell the aggregator that we need so
many thousand tonnes, so many

lakh tonnes. The aggregators get it
from the farmers,” he said.

Paddy straw is used as feedstock in 2G ethanol plants, as biomass for biogas plants and to make
pellets and briquettes for industrial and power-plant fuel. Paper and
cardboard units also use it.

Amarjeet Singh, who farms

10 acres, said smaller farmers are
still struggling to arrange a baler.
“Getting a baler is the problem. It
needs lots of connections,” he said.
With paddy at different stages of
maturity, he said, machine hiring
is currently easier because there is
less demand. “At present, the renting of the machines is less because
paddy in most of the fields is yet to
mature. The rent is now Rs 700 per
acre, but it will go up when every
field is yellow,” he said, adding that
mid-Oct will be the real test of the
machinery’s reach.

Farmers said machinery could
cost around Rs 2,400 an acre at peak

demand. Karamveer, who farms
four acres in Jind, said farmers
already facing losses could not afford the expense. “We have spent a
lot on crops and we are at a loss so
we can’t afford to rent machines,”
he said, referring to higher fertiliser costs and an indifferent monsoon that has hit crop yield.

Balbir Singh, a farmer in Narwana, said private operators prioritise larger farms. “If a farmer
has only one or two acres, no one
goes to collect it. They say, ‘I have
to travel so far; the fuel cost alone
will be too high.’ The small farmer

suffers the most,” he said.

Nagpal said the department was trying to identify vulnerable farmers and
match machinery with their
harvest schedules. “Small
and marginal farmers are
most vulnerable as they lack
resources,” he said. “Our
field staff are locating them
to find out when they need
the machines,” he said. On
staggered
harvesting,
said: “The staggered harvesting is there in the whole district. Which block is harvesting first, which one later, we
have a complete calendar.”

The number of red-zone
villages
(those
reporting
most fires) fell from 14 in 2024
to three in 2025, while yellowzone villages declined from
273 to 145. Additional chief secretary (agriculture) Vijayender Kumar said the state is not predicting
a fire-free season. “At the moment,
no one can predict if this is the
year that Haryana will see no farm
fires, because Haryana is a state
with lots of farmers and there are
several issues involved,” he said.

Halloween,

Levity aside, the two-hourplus gathering brought together an extraordinary concentration of tech and financial power: Pichai, Elon Musk, Mark
Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Microsoft’s
Satya Nadella, Micron’s Sanjay Mehrotra, Palantir’s Shyam Sankar, Palo Alto Networks’ Nikesh Arora, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, executives from AMD, Broadcom and

It was quite a lineup — essentially the people who make

First, companies are to
monitor their models for
risks, including cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical
threats, and ensure they do
not breach or access technical systems in unintended
ways. Second, an internal team is supposed to check whether those safeguards actually
work. Third comes an independent external auditor or
evaluator. And fourth, an independent board committee
is supposed to review the findings and press for fixes.

The companies also agreed
to meet regularly to develop
common standards, with the
possibility that the principles
could eventually be turned into law or regulation. For now,
though, the accord is voluntary and contains no penalties,
no reporting deadlines and no
requirement that audit results
be made public.

Trump called it “almost

supplied the less diplomatic

world will keep an eye on each
other” — a proposition that did
not exactly allay fears of AI

tech oligarchy and their patron in the White House are playing with fire. “When a handful of billionaire monopolists

deployed safely and securely,”
gushed Palo Alto Networks’
Nikesh Arora.

“The White House Accord
and the Joint Commitment
on Frontier Responsibilities
signed today...contains real
tangible steps to promote safe
development, while delivering the economic and scientific benefits of this technology,” asserted Pichai.

But somewhere, one imagines, AI algos were taking
notes, drafting minutes and
smirking to themselves about
who the joke was on.

New Delhi: The number of
people engaged in formal manufacturing sector increased
by nearly 14 lakh in 2024-25 to
2.1 crore, along with robust
growth recorded in wages paid to workers, value addition
and investment, latest Annual
Survey of Industries (ASI) released Wednesday showed.

Wages paid directly to workers surpassed profit made by
the factories. Wages rose 13%
to Rs 3.8 lakh crore from Rs 3.4
lakh crore, while total emoluments, including bonus, increased 12.1% to Rs 8 lakh crore.
On the other hand, total profits
rose 7.7% to Rs 11.6 lakh crore.

The number of factories in
the country increased to nearly 2.7 lakh from 2.6 lakh in
2023-24, with the highest number of establishments reported in Tamil Nadu (41,221), followed by Gujarat (33,084), Maharashtra (27,379) and Uttar
Pradesh (24,964).

During the same period,
gross value added (GVA), which
represents productivity of a
sector, rose nearly 10% to Rs 26.9
lakh crore from Rs 24.6 lakh crore. In terms of individual share
of states in all India GVA, Maharashtra (16%) recorded the
highest GVA, followed by Gujarat (14.1%), Tamil Nadu (10.9%),
Karnataka (7.3%) and Uttar
Pradesh (6.6%). These five states accounted for more than 54
% of the total manufacturing
GVA in the country.

In terms of industries — basic metals, motor vehicles, chemicals and chemical products,
pharmaceuticals and food products — together accounted for
more than 45% of total manufacturing GVA in 2024-25. Fixed
capital which represents the
long term, physical assets used
by enterprises for production
rose 10.5% to Rs 51.1 lakh crore.

Fresh from scripting history with their maiden Ranji
Trophy triumph, Jammu
& Kashmir now stand on the
threshold of another landmark
achievement. Hosting the biggest match in the state’s domestic cricket history, J&Kwill

look to complete a rare double
when they take on a formidable
Rest of India side, led by India’s
Test vice-captain and wicketkeeper-batter Rishabh Pant, in
the Irani Cup at Srinagar’s picturesque Sher-i-Kashmir Stadium from Thursday.

The J&K Cricket Association has allowed free, though
restricted, entry for spectators, and the home side can expect strong backing from a
crowd of around 3,000.

Yet, despite
its traditional
prestige,
Irani Cup has
struggled for attention
this
year amid a
crowded calendar. India’s T20
squad is at the Asian Games,
another national side is engaged in an ODI series against
the West Indies, while several
fringe players are representing
India A against Australia A in
Puducherry. As a result, a fixture once viewed as a key audition for India’s Test team has
lost some of its relevance, serving largely as valuable red-ball
preparation for Pant.

While Pant’s presence will
draw the spotlight, the selectors and team management will
be equally interested in Akash
Deep’s comeback. The Bengal
pacer returns after seven
months on the sidelines due to
lower-back stress fracture. The
injury interrupted a promising
Test career, highlighted by his
match haul of 10-187 in India’s
thumping win over England at
Edgbaston in July 2025.

Srinagar: Giant billboards
greet visitors entering the
Jammu & Kashmir Cricket
Association premises in Srinagar’s
high-security
Church Lane.

One features local cricketer Auqib Nabi, highlighting
his Ranji performance and
describing him as India’s
No.1 fast bowler. Another celebrates the Jammu and Kashmir team as Ranji champions.

The Sher-i-Kashmir stadium opens into a setting of towering chinar trees, with the
Zabarwan mountain range
visible ahead.

Many describe it the country’s most beautiful cricket
ground. Preparations for the
Irani Cup, scheduled to start
here from Thursday, are being given final touches. In the
5,000-capacity stadium invitations for the matches have
been sent to a select audience,
officials said, citing the stadium’s past history. “We don’t
want to take any chances,” an
official said. Only one gate
would be used as the main entry point, while the others
would remain closed.

On Oct 13, 1983, during the
first international cricket
match here between India
and the visiting West Indies,
the Indian team — having
won the World Cup only a few
months before — faced an unexpected reaction from the
crowd. The newly crowned
world champion team was
booed by sections of the
crowd, while the West Indies
cricketers — who won the
game — unexpectedly felt at

home in the Valley. Former
captain Sunil Gavaskar later
wrote in ‘Runs ’n’ Ruins’ that
being hooted at after a defeat
is understandable, but this
was incredible. He also said
there were many in the crowd
shouting pro-Pakistan slogans which confounded them
as they were playing the West
Indies, and not Pakistan.

A
similar
controversy
erupted in Sept 1986 during a
match between Australia and
India at the same venue. Some
youths dug up the pitch,
prompting police to register
an FIR during the initial
stages of the game. The accused were later arrested on
charges of damaging the
pitch. Against this backdrop,
the Irani Cup will headline a

Guwahati: Shubman Gill produced a batting masterclass as
he smashed the fastest double
century in the history of ODI
cricket to help India chase West
Indies’ imposing 406-run target
with 39 balls to spare in the
second ODI at Barsapara
Cricket Stadium here on
Wednesday. The eight-wicket
win also sealed the three-match
series in the hosts’ favour.

Gill remained unbeaten on
223 off just 133 balls, with 28
fours and eight sixes. He
brought up his double hundred
off 117 balls, eclipsing Ishan
Kishan’s previous mark of a
126-ball double century against
Bangladesh in Dec 2022. It was
Gill’s second ODI double hundred. He is now behind only
Rohit Sharma in the list of
Indian batters with multiple

double centuries. Gill reached
his 11th ODI century in just 62
balls, setting the tone for an
extraordinary chase. He found
boundaries at will, scoring all
around the park as India never
let the West Indies settle down.

At the other end, Rohit
Sharma provided the perfect
launchpad with a 101 off 75
balls. The opener completed
his 35th ODI century. In the
process, he crossed 12,000 runs
in the format, becoming only
the third Indian after Sachin
Tendulkar and Virat Kohli and
the seventh batter overall to
reach the milestone.

Rohit was dismissed immediately after reaching three
figures, trapped LBW by
Jayden Seales. He had earlier
been given a reprieve on 84
when Keacy Carty dropped
him at deep mid-wicket.

Gill and Rohit’s opening

stand of 255 runs fell just three
runs short of Sachin Tendulkar and Sourav Ganguly’s
all-time record of 258 runs for
the first wicket which they registered against Kenya in 2001.

Virat Kohli made 29 before
holing out at deep backward
point while attempting to guide
a bouncer. Gill, however, remained in command. His unbeaten knock carried India to
406/2 and their highest successful ODI chase, surpassing their
previous best of 362/1 against
Australia in Jaipur in 2013.

India’s remarkable pursuit
followed an powerful batting
display from West Indies, who
posted 405/7 — their highest
ODI total against India. For the
first time in their ODI history,
three West Indies batters
scored centuries in the same
innings. John Campbell struck
101 off 68 balls, captain Shai

Hope made 104 off 94, while
Amir Jangoo top-scored with
114 off 77 balls. Jangoo continued his fine run after an unbeaten half-century in the
opening ODI.

overs (R Sharma 101, S Gill 233
not out; S Joseph 1/52) by 8
wickets.

New Delhi: Apple is entering India’s UPI-first payments market with a distinctly card-led play, counting on rising contactless
usage, wider NFC acceptance and regulatory support for
biometric authentication to
create space for Apple Pay.

Rather than trying to displace UPI, Apple is positioning the service as an additional payment option for iPhone users, who already use credit and debit cards. Jennifer
Bailey, Apple’s vice-president
of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet, said the timing reflects
how much India’s payments
ecosystem has evolved.

“India offers a digitally
savvy demographic, and the
broader mobile payments
ecosystem has grown significantly in recent years,”
Bailey told TOI. “NFC acceptance has expanded meaningfully with the majority of POS systems in India
being
NFC-capable,
card usage is growing.”

Apple Pay will initially
work with Visa and Mastercard credit cards issued by
Axis Bank, with Apple looking to add more issuing
banks as they become technically ready to support the service. It plans to progressively
widen access through additional banking partnerships.

At launch, users will be
able to tap and pay at thousands of NFC-enabled merchant locations, including Tata and Reliance brands, Chaayos, Le15, Comet, House of
Masaba and Apple Stores.
Apple Pay will be available
for online transactions on
apps including Blinkit, Ixigo,
MakeMyTrip, Zepto and Zomato. Apple is pointing to
RBI’s framework on authentication mechanisms for digital payment transactions as
an important development.

payment option with Apple Pay

The caveats filed by Tata

Trusts are a bid to
avoid a repeat of the ex
parte order the charity commissioner issued in May barring Sir Ratan Tata Trust
(SRTT), the second-largest
Tata Sons shareholder, from
holding board meetings after Srinivasan complained
that its board composition
violated the Maharashtra
Public Trusts Act.

This time, Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT), the largest
Tata Sons shareholder, and
the five other Trusts have filed caveats under Sections
41D and 47 of the Act, which
govern the removal of trustees and suspension of the
board, and Section 41E,
which relates to restraining
dealings in trust property.

In his latest complaint,
Srinivasan has asked the
commissioner to open an inquiry into SDTT’s governance. He also asked the commissioner to bar SDTT from
holding
board
meetings,
freeze changes to its board
and reserve the option of
suspending or removing its
trustees if violations were
found.

Tata
Group
watchers
said the orders Srinivasan
sought, if granted, could incapacitate SDTT too. With
SRTT already under the May
ban, SDTT and SRTT would
both be constrained from
functioning normally and
exercising their shareholder
rights in Tata Sons on crucial matters.

Srinivasan also sought
directions from the commissioner requiring Noel Tata
to recuse himself from decisions on appointing nominees to Tata Sons’ AGMs, be
barred from exercising the
Trusts’ voting rights at those
meetings, and be prevented,
as a nominee director, from
taking part in Tata Sons
board decisions.

As evidence of interference, Srinivasan pointed to
Noel’s involvement in talks
on liquidity for Shapoorji
Pallonji (SP) Group and a

proposal to monetise part of
its Tata Sons stake. Noel
sought authorisation for Tata Sons operating team and
Trusts to continue negotiating with SP Group and bankers. Srinivasan has said that
amounts to Trusts taking a
direct role in substantial
commercial
transactions
concerning Tata Sons.

He also cited Trusts’ public opposition to a Tata Sons
listing, saying they had resolved that Tata Sons should
stay unlisted and told the
company to implement that
position. He also alleged
SDTT tried to influence his
independent judgment as
Trusts’ nominee director on

Tata Sons board. Earlier this
month, a resolution was circulated to stop him participating in or voting on the
proposed listing. He characterised the move as an attempt to suppress dissenting
views and concentrate decision-making power within a
smaller group of trustees.

He also questioned the
basis of Noel’s chairmanship of Trusts and the circumstances
surrounding
the appointment of his son,
Neville Tata, to SDTT’s
board in Nov 2025, including
what he described as “my exclusion from the decisionmaking process.”

Srinivasan argued that
Trusts’ involvement in Tata
Sons’ commercial affairs
could jeopardise their income-tax exemptions and expose them to tax on accreted
income. Given the value of
SDTT’s Tata Sons stake, he
said the consequences for its
charitable corpus could be
immense.

The May order had already put a question mark
over Tata Sons annual general meeting (AGM). The AoA
require SDTT and SRTT to
jointly appoint a nominee to
represent their shareholding before the AGM can be
held. SRTT cannot act because of the commissioner’s
order. The AGM must also
approve
Chandrasekaran’s continuation as a Tata
Sons
director,
Trusts,
excluding
SRTT,
hold the votes to influence
that outcome.

Mumbai: Ahead of the introduction of MDR or merchant discount rate fees on
UPI transactions over Rs
2,000, bank chiefs have provided assurance that everyday
consumers and small merchants will be protected. At
the same time, the fees are expected to increase penetration of UPI and new features
like credit on UPI will drive
business growth.

“The biggest benefit is
that UPI remains completely
free for consumers. There is
no MDR for customers,” said
Debadatta Chand, managing
director & CEO of Bank of Baroda. He added that, with the
Rs 2,000 transaction value set
as the floor, small merchants
also continue to be protected.
“In fact, around 96% of merchant transactions by volume
are expected to remain unaffected,” he said.

Echoing this stance, Rajnish Karnatak, chief of Bank
of India, emphasised the limited reach of the fee on everyday users. “Most people will
not feel the impact of the MDR
because merchant transactions under Rs 2,000, peer-topeer transfers, and autopay
mandates remain completely
free,” Karnatak stated. “This
small, targeted fee is about reinvesting into the system to
build a more secure, high-speed, and resilient infrastructure that ultimately benefits the
public.”

“Banks are making significant investments to support the UPI ecosystem. These costs include technology
infrastructure, transaction

processing,
cybersecurity,
fraud monitoring, dispute
resolution
customer
support,” Chand noted. “As
usage continues to increase,
investments will also need to
keep pace to maintain a secure and seamless experience,”
he said.

Chand added that the
next phase of growth hinges
on these investments: “The
next phase is about reaching
more people, particularly in
rural and semi-urban India,
bringing more merchants
onto digital payments and introducing new use cases.”

Karnatak took a similar
view of technical expenditures: “We view our digital
spending as a strategic investment rather than just a
cost. We have been investing
heavily in upgrading our IT
infrastructure, and as digital
transaction volumes grow,
including UPI volumes.”

To soften the transition
on merchants, Indian Bank
is introducing fee waivers
monitoring
mechanisms. Indian Bank MD &
CEO Binod Kumar confirmed that the bank is considering waiving acquiring bank
charges to reduce the MDR
impact on merchants.

Indian Bank will activate
an internal mechanism within days to monitor UPI
transactions after MDR introduction, tracking amounts charged to customers
and flagging discrepancies.
Banks are also expanding
Credit on UPI and proprietary apps. Bank of Baroda said
Credit on UPI will enable customers to use pre-approved
credit lines for payments.

New Delhi: Carmakers will get
awider set of options to meet India’s tighter fuel-efficiency requirements from April 2027,
with the final Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE-III)
norms offering incentives for
EVs and hybrids, a weight-sensitive target formula and the
ability to trade compliance credits. The new norms will apply
to new passenger vehicles manufactured or imported for sale
in India. The rules, notified by
the power ministry, will run until March 2032 and progressively tighten fleet-level fuel-efficiency targets.

Instead of setting the same
target for every company, the
permitted fuel consumption is
linked to the average weight of
vehicles in a manufacturer’s
portfolio. The final formula flattens the target curve, giving
lighter fleets relatively softer
targets than earlier proposals
while requiring greater efficiency improvements from heavier vehicles. A separate concession earlier proposed for small
petrol cars hasbeen dropped.

The framework could influence product strategies as manufacturers balance small cars,
SUVs and cleaner powertrains
to meet their fleet averages. Battery EVs and range-extended
EVs receive a 3x super-credit,
while plug-in hybrids and flexfuel strong hybrids get 2.5x and
strong hybrids 1.6x, effectively
allowing sales of cleaner vehicles to carry greater weight in
compliance calculations.

Rahul Bharti, senior executive officer, corporate affairs at
Maruti Suzuki, said, “The regulation recognises the contribution of multiple powertrain
technologies and fuels, encouraging multi-faceted R&Dand
innovation.” He added that the
credit-debit mechanism is an
improvement over CAFE-II.

Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles MD & CEO Shailesh
Chandra said, “The continued
recognition of zero-emission
technologies reinforces the critical role of electrification in
achieving India’s long-term decarbonisation objectives.”

CAFE-III: Car
cos get more
options to meet

efficiency rules

Bengaluru:
Electric
twowheeler maker Simple Energy has raised Rs 1,750 crore
($180 million) in an all-equity
Series Cround, as the Bengaluru-based company looks to
scale manufacturing, distribution and product development amid intensifying competition in the EV market.

The round was led by the
family office of Thyrocare founder Arokiaswamy Velumani, with participation from founder and CEO Suhas Rajkumar, co-founder and CFO Ankit Gupta, Bengaluru-based
HNI Amit Mishra and the Haran Family Office. Simple has
now raised over Rs 2,530 crore
in total. Simple currently has
installed production capacity
of 10,000 units a month, according to its updated release. Cofounder Shreshth Mishra told
TOI that actual production is

currently around 2,500 vehicles a month, while retail sales
are roughly 1,800-2,000 units.
The company is seeing monthly demand of around 4,000-
4,500 vehicles, he said.
“Demand is almost double
of what we are able to supply,”
Mishra said. Simple plans to
eventually take monthly manufacturing capacity to around 30,000 units and above,
while expanding its network
across tier-I and tier-II cities.

This Asian Games, India have
failed to defend at least a
dozen gold medals won
across sports in the previous
Games in Hangzhou. Forms and fortunes have fluctuated.

At the Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park
Multipurpose Park here, the weather
swung from cool to hot to cloudy, but
the Indians remained unruffled. Youngsters stood up to be counted, seasoned
campaigners brought their experience
to the fore, and a meticulous system
ensured little was left to chance.

There were no upsets, no pull-outs
and no excuses. Just precision and
performance, a heady combination
that helped India sweep the women’s,
mixed and men’s team compound gold
medals. The icing on the cake, the
mixed team of Chikitha Taniparthi
and Sahil Jadhav punching their
ticket for the 2028 LA Olympics.

For much of the day, it felt like listening to a favourite song on repeat.
The same rhythm, over and over. Semifinals, finals, women, men, mixed. Finish one event, move to the next and
reproduce the performance.

First up were Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Chikitha and Prithika Pradeep,
who defeated China 238-234 in the
women’s final after edging South Korea 234-233 in the semifinals.

In the process, they matched South
Korea’s world record score, dating
back to 2014.

It was teamwork in its truest sense.
In the final, when Prithika shot a nine
in the second game, her teammates compensated. It was the
pattern throughout the contest
— one faltered, the others stepped
up. They backed each other and
looked completely in control, even
when the pressure mounted.

“We spent a lot of time meditating
and visualising. We stayed focused and
thought of going up on the podium and
the Indian flag going up. That was our
aim and we are glad to have achieved
it,” said debutant Pune teenager Prithika, who turned 18 three days ago.

At the heart of the celebrations
was seasoned campaigner Jyothi,
from Challapalli in Andhra, who was
also part of the gold-medal winning
team in Hangzhou.

“This is the first time we got to
play against China in the women’s

team contest. We were there for each
other and motivating one another to
give our best in each shot. We were
there to fight till our very last arrow,”
said the 30-year-old.

There was barely any time to savour the victory. Chikitha, 21, quickly
turned her attention to the mixed
team event with Jadhav.

The pair began with a 156-155 semifinal win over Thailand before a
nervy final against South Korea. They
started strongly, producing 10 straight
perfect scores to take a two-point lead
into the final four arrows.

Then came a wobble. India
managed 39 while Korea shot 40,
leaving the scores tied at 157-all
and forcing a shoot-off. The Indians responded with composure,
producing twin 10s. Korea could manage 19, leaving India with another gold.

In the men’s event, Kushal Dalal,
Jadhav and Ganesh Mani Rathnam
brushed aside South Korea 239-236 in
the last-four contest before edging
China 238-237 in a tense final.

Even when they trailed by two
points, the Indians refused to allow
the sweep to slip away.

The results were the product of
preparation that left little to chance.
Ahead of the Games, the team spent
15 days at a simulated venue at the
Sports Authority of India centre in
Sonipat, complete with the screens,

targets and podiums that would be
used in Okazaki. Crowd noise and
music systems were also introduced
to replicate the atmosphere they
would encounter in competition.

Former India coach Sergio Pagni
watched from the sidelines, while his
successor, highly accomplished
American Dave Cousins, who took

charge in June, soaked in the success
alongside team coach Jiwanjot Singh.

Cousins credited the sweep to the
team’s passion. “It’s a youthful team
with a lot of good energy and passion.
Passion is very important because it
isn’t something you can manufacture.
It has to come from within, especially
at such a young age. We were bold.”

complacency.

league match against Bangladesh. Travelling reserve Nilakanta Sharma will take his 
place in the squad.

their last Asian Games meeting, when they thrashed Pakistan 10-2 in the league phase in 
2023, but in the recent FIH

sweat for 5-3 victory.

our preparation, playing together and giving everything 
for India. We want to earn our 
place in the final.”

In the other semifinal, Malaysia take on South Korea.

hockey team have found a way to keep 
moving forward this year — make mistakes, make up for them and keep battling.

Up against a stubborn South Korea 
who defended in numbers and refused to 
give an inch, India had to grind their way 
through the semifinal before emerging 
2-0 winners and booking a gold-medal 
clash against China.

India’s reward is a final against China, who survived a shootout against 
hosts Japan after their semifinal ended

goalless. China won 4-2 in the shootout.

avenge their semifinal defeat to China 
from the previous Asian Games. More 
importantly, the gold medal carries the 
added prize of an Olympic berth.

The previous edition’s bronze medallists finally broke the deadlock through

before captain Salima Tete doubled the 
lead four minutes later.

For long stretches, though, it was a 
test of India’s patience. They dominated possession and made repeated 
circle entries, but South Korea’s goalkeeper Seoyeon Lee stood firm. The 
Koreans were content to sit deep and 
frustrate their opponents. India had 11 
penalty corners but converted only one 
— a statistic that will hardly please 
drag-flick coach and legendary Dutchman Taeke Taekema. But the job, ultimately, was done.

With most of the action unfolding in 
the Korean half, Salima and company 
occasionally appeared to second-guess 
their moves. South Korea, meanwhile, 
offered little going forward, with attacking moves few and far between.

India returned after the break 
with greater purpose and were rewarded in the 44th minute. On their 
eighth penalty corner, a variation 
worked perfectly, with Ishika getting the 
final touch to deflect the ball into the net.

Four minutes later, India had breathing room. Salima’s run down the right 
flank ended with her effort taking a deflection off a Korean stick and finding the 
net. South Korea finally opened up in the 
closing stages and earned a last-minute 
penalty corner, but failed to make it count.

s AI reshapes music-making and viral hits increasingly influence what listeners consume, 
Grammy-winner Shankar Mahadevan believes the biggest challenge facing music is not technology or changing trends, but the loss of musical 
craft. In a conversation with us, the singer-composer, who has given us hugely popular songs in films 
like Dil Chahta Hai, My Name Is Khan, Dil 
Dhadakne Do, Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna, speaks 
about the creative freedom offered by independent music and why, despite decades of success 
and global recognition, music itself remains his 
greatest reward.

In an era of AI-generated music 
and viral hits, what worries you 
most about the future of music?
There is nothing wrong with viral 
hits, and there is nothing wrong 
with using AI, provided it is used 
responsibly and ethically. What 
worries me is when people 
stop learning the craft. I 
hope we continue to have 
students of music who 
want to understand the 
nuances, the origins of 
melodies, ragas, talas, the 
mathematics of music and 
the incredible richness 
of our musical traditions. 
Music, like engineering, 
painting or dance, deserves 
deep study. That is what I 
hope never disappears.
SHANKAR MAHADEVAN

The Grammy, global recognition, success and fame are all just 
by-products of music. Music itself never fails to surprise me. When I

Beyond K-Pop, Korea displays its 
cultural legacy at the British Museum
Korea’s cultural story takes centre stage at the British Museum with a new exhibition exploring more than 2,000 years of 
the country’s artistic heritage beyond the global phenomenon of K-pop. Opening October 1 and running until January 31, 2027, 
the exhibition brings together works dating from around 400 BC to 
the present. Contemporary works include Yeesookyung’s Translated Vase series, a sculpture assembled from shards  discarded by potters, and Suh Do Ho’s Self-Portrait, which explores imperfection, migration and belonging. Curator Sang-ah Kim commented to Reuters, 
“Most people, especially young people in the UK, know about Korea 
through its popular culture...They may not know Korea has a long 
history, of 2,000 years of creativity, resilience and technical skill.”

Every time we
write about
coffee, we receive a mix of passionate reminders
and gentle rebukes from our readers:
real coffee isn’t just what you see on
your Instagram feed, nor is it confined
to chic cafés serving pineapple-fermented pourovers in minimalist ceramic
cups. Decades before a new generation
“discovered” specialty roasts, coffee
culture was already deeply woven into
the daily rhythm of South India –
served piping hot in signature brass or
stainless steel dabarah and tumbler
sets engineered to aerate, cool, froth,
and savour every last sip of filter kaapi.

Unlike third-wave coffee cultures
across the globe that treat the bean
with clinical isolation, South Indian
filter kaapi – crafted from beans nurtured in the shade-grown estates of
the Western Ghats (across
Chikmagalur, Coorg, Wayanad, and
the Nilgiris) and brewed using a traditional metal drip filter—makes no
apologies for what it is. Bold, chicory-infused, decoction-strong, milky,
and distinctively sweet, it has held
its ground against wave after wave
of transient global trends. (One can
only gawp at the sheer absurdity of
“iced coffee infusion” IV bags served

at gimmick cafés.)

Moreover, filter kaapi,
with its instantly recognisable aroma and taste,
has been travelling remarkably well beyond
the traditional breakfast
table. Its signature flavour profile now infuses
everything from artisanal ice creams, popsicles, and panna cottas to
craft chocolates.

Which brings us to
the imperative of owning it, embracing it,
and reminding the
world of how we took the legendary
seven seeds smuggled from Yemen
by Baba Budan centuries ago and
made the brew entirely our own.
While raw regional beans like Coorg
Arabica, Bababudangiri Arabica, or
Wayanad Robusta have rightly
earned their individual Geographical Indication (GI) tags over the
years, the cup itself remains unrecognised.

Ergo, the question. Should South
Indian Filter Kaapi get GI tagged?
Not just for the raw agricultural ingredients, which have already been acknowledged,
but for the process, the decoction ritual, and the
unique culinary technique. Not very different from Neapolitan pizza making or traditional
Belgian beer brewing. Because filter
kaapi after all, is an irreplaceable,
region-rooted cultural IP.

It is International Coffee Day
and while we celebrate how the
world keeps reinventing coffee, and
finds newer ways to brew a cup, we
may want to pause, sip some filter
kaapi and reflect on how South
India simply keeps perfecting what’s
in the dabarah.

Before coffee, there was kaapi

Do you think today’s musicians are 
under more pressure to chase 
trends over creating timeless music? 
The pressure isn’t self-induced. It often comes from the industry, especially in film music. But independent 
music is a different story. Artistes today are creating fabulous music because they have complete creative 
control. Nobody tells them to add or 
remove an instrument or change the  
composition. That freedom allows 
timeless music to emerge naturally.
After a Grammy, global 
recognition and decades of 
success, what is the one thing

music still gives you that fame 
never can? 
The Grammy, global recognition, 
success and fame are all just byproducts of music. Music itself never fails to surprise me. When I hear 
a great artiste perform, I feel humbled and think... Should I go back to 
the drawing board and start learning again? Even when I hear my 
own compositions, I sometimes 
wonder… did I actually create this? 
What was my state of mind then? 
That process of creation and the 
beauty of experiencing music can 
never be compared with awards or 
recognition. Music itself is the 
greatest reward.

You’ve spent decades performing across 
genres and generations. Do you feel Indian 
audiences are increasingly looking for 
experiences that offer meaning, connection 
and reflection, rather than just entertainment? 
Indian audiences today enjoy the complete concert experience 
– music, stage production, lights, graphics and technology. But 
that is only one aspect of it. If you look at a global band like 
Shakti, there are no pyrotechnics or elaborate visuals during 
performances. The experience is purely musical. The same is true 
of great classical concerts by legends like Hariprasad Chaurasia 
or artists like Kaushiki Chakraborty. There are no ﬁreworks, yet 
the impact is extraordinary. Audiences today appreciate both 
kinds of experiences. Ultimately, it is the music that creates the 
deepest connection.

You’ve spent decades performing across 
genres and generations. Do you feel Indian 
audiences are increasingly looking for 
experiences that offer meaning, connection 
and reflection, rather than just entertainment? 
Indian audiences today enjoy the complete concert experience 
– music, stage production, lights, graphics and technology. But 
that is only one aspect of it. If you look at a global band like 
Shakti, there are no pyrotechnics or elaborate visuals during 
performances. The experience is purely musical. The same is true 
of great classical concerts by legends like Hariprasad Chaurasia 
or artists like Kaushiki Chakraborty. There are no ﬁreworks, yet 
the impact is extraordinary. Audiences today appreciate both 
kinds of experiences. Ultimately, it is the music that creates the 
deepest connection.
